docs.lead_paragraph: Your average vintage clothing shop does not come with the warning “Mind Your Head When Leaving Seat.” It’s sound advice at Lodekka, a recently opened boutique in the North Williams neighborhood of Portland, Ore., housed inside in an eggshell white two-story Bristol Lodekka bus. The bus itself — built in 1965 for the citizens of Liverpool — has been exhaustively remodeled in shades of almond, coral pink and warm red. The exterior can’t help but catch eyes (and foot traffic from the nearby brunch spots), but it’s the selection inside that tugs at the bargain hunter’s heartstrings: midcentury Oleg Cassini dresses for $12, a pair of purple Halston pumps for $7 and men’s western wear culled from the high deserts of eastern Oregon. Comfortable, not cluttered, Lodekka is also home to trunks full of yellowing National Park maps, McCall’s pattern books from the early ’80s, Brownie Twin 20 Kodak cameras and a curator’s closet of Pendleton skirts and button-ups — this is Portland, after all.

headline.main: Bus Stop | Lodekka Dress Shop

docs.abstract: Those who insist on a linear narrative may find themselves puzzled by “Uncle Boonmee.” But encountered in a certain frame of mind, it can produce something close to bliss.
docs.snippet: Those who insist on a linear narrative may find themselves puzzled by “Uncle Boonmee.” But encountered in a certain frame of mind, it can produce something close to bliss.
docs.lead_paragraph: Last May, when a Cannes Film Festival jury headed by Tim Burton awarded the Palme d’Or to “Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives,” there was widespread surprise and a few eruptions of outrage. The film — from the Thai director Apichatpong Weerasethakul, who has become a familiar presence on the festival circuit over the past decade — is unquestionably strange, at times mystifyingly oblique. Those who insist on a linear narrative or an easily identifiable set of themes may find themselves puzzled, perhaps to the point of frustration. But it is hard to see how this movie, with its contemplative mood and genial, curious spirit, could make anybody angry. On the contrary: encountered in an appropriately exploratory frame of mind, it can produce something close to bliss.

headline.main: A Farewell to This Life, and All Its Ghosts

docs.snippet: Region by region, plate by plate and glass by glass, the new book “Italy Dish by Dish” provides definitions and background for thousands of items.
docs.lead_paragraph: The subtitle of Monica Sartoni Cesari’s “Italy Dish by Dish” (“A Comprehensive Guide to Eating in Italy”) only tells part of the story. The chunky new book, with the dimensions of a nice portion of lasagna, is really a guide to Italian food no matter where you eat it. Region by region, plate by plate and glass by glass, it provides definitions and background for thousands of items. So if you see porceddu on a menu, you can discover that it’s Sardinian suckling pig. There’s a basic recipe for each region, like the bucatini all’amatriciana for Lazio. Among other minor gaps, Ligurians may quibble that their focaccia gets short shrift, but that’s not to take away from the usefulness of this volume.

headline.main: A Hefty Guide to Eating Italian

docs.lead_paragraph: Using its emergency authority, the Drug Enforcement Administration on Tuesday announced a temporary ban of five chemicals used to make synthetic marijuana products, which have grown increasingly popular over the past few years. The ban, which the drug agency said it would pursue in 2010, will remain in effect for at least a year until it is determined whether the chemicals should be permanently controlled. Fake marijuana products produce a high similar to marijuana when smoked. The products  typically sold at smoke shops  have caused numerous health problems including seizures and hallucinations, the drug agency has said.

docs.lead_paragraph: An anti-gang dragnet has led to the arrest of 678 gang members and their associates, most of them immigrants, in 168 cities, federal officials announced Tuesday. The three-month-long operation focused on groups with ties to international drug trafficking, said officials from Immigration and Customs Enforcement, an arm of the Department of Homeland Security. Some 447 of the defendants were charged with crimes while the rest were arrested for administrative immigration violations, officials said. The offensive was part of a five-year campaign by immigration officials to combat violent street gangs by prosecuting and deporting their members.

docs.lead_paragraph: Lori Berenson has always loved to walk. When she was a high-school student in Manhattan in the mid-1980s, she walked home at night from her job at Pasta & Cheese, on the Upper East Side, to the apartment where she grew up, on East 25th Street. When she began her prison sentence in Peru, in 1996, for collaborating with a terrorist group, convicted terrorists had to spend 23½ hours a day inside their cells. Even then, Berenson walked in the 6-by-9-foot space she and another woman shared — two steps forward, two steps backward — for hours. “People ask, what did you miss most?” she said in August, two and a half months after she was released on parole, having served nearly 15 years of a 20-year sentence. “This was definitely it.”

docs.abstract: A new film adapts Oliver Sacks’s account of how music helped spur a man’s damaged memory.
docs.snippet: A new film adapts Oliver Sacks’s account of how music helped spur a man’s damaged memory.
docs.lead_paragraph: We lost a lot of brain cells out on the road with the Grateful Dead, but maybe we gained some, too. Witness “The Music Never Stopped,” a film adaptation of Oliver Sacks’s account of a man who is unable to store new memories after a brain tumor ravages his frontal lobe. It is discovered that music — particularly the Dead’s — is able to penetrate the barrier ever so slightly and help the man to reconnect with himself and his family. Some facts (some big ones) from Sacks’s essay, “The Last Hippie,” seem to have been altered and molded into a workable movie narrative, naturally, and I worry that Sacks’s poignantly honest account will have received a Hollywood face-lift. But maybe the film will surprise us, as did the melancholy but still-hopeful ending to “Awakenings.”

headline.main: If You Get Confused, Listen to the Music Play

docs.abstract: Adele, the British singer who won the Grammy Award for best new artist two years ago, is the big winner on the Billboard chart this week.
docs.snippet: Adele, the British singer who won the Grammy Award for best new artist two years ago, is the big winner on the Billboard chart this week.
docs.lead_paragraph: Adele, the British singer who won the Grammy Award for best new artist two years ago, is the big winner on the Billboard chart this week, with a No. 1 opening for her new album and a rebound for her last one. Adele’s new album, “21” (XL/Columbia), opened with 352,000 sales, according to Nielsen SoundScan. Thanks to a blitz of television appearances to promote the album, that was the best opening-week sales of any album in three months. (In the interim, there have been some painfully low numbers.) And her debut album, “19,” bolted 34 spots to No. 16, with 18,000 sales. But almost everything else on the chart is a loser. Last week’s No. 1, Justin Bieber’s “Never Say Never: The Remixes” (Island), fell to No. 2 with 102,000, a 38 percent decline, and Mr. Bieber’s “My World 2.0,” at No. 5, lost 22 percent. Mumford & Sons’ “Sigh No More” (Glassnote), at No. 3, dropped 46 percent; “Now That’s What I Call Music!” Vol. 37 is No. 4 with a 38 percent loss; Bruno Mars’s “Doo-Wops & Hooligans” (Elektra), at No. 6, lost 40 percent, and so on. Last week’s numbers were higher than usual because of the traditional retail boost the week after the Grammys. But that only underlines the scale of Adele’s success. On the digital singles chart, Lady Gaga’s “Born This Way,” which was enormously popular out of the gate, lost 44 percent of its sales in its third week, with 286,000, although that was enough for it to hold at No. 1.

headline.main: Adele Is No. 1

I don’t want to get into the specifics of Forbes’s argument here — it’s pretty boilerplate stuff — but I do want to call your attention to a recent Rolling Stone article about Carter. It’s not an apologia, far from it. But it complicates our understanding of our 39th president in necessary ways. By the end of the article — and if you have the patience, the end of the essay Carter’s old speechwriter Hendrik Hertzberg wrote about him way back when — Carter will feel to you much more like a real man, not just a punching bag who is trotted out every now and again to boost Web stats.

docs.lead_paragraph: When Andi O’Conor’s house in the foothills west of Boulder, Colo., burned down last September, she began to blog. The Fourmile Canyon wildfire had started one very dry, windy day, sparked by an improperly extinguished fire pit, investigators believe. Flames ravaged the foothills and meadows for 11 days, blackening more than 6,000 acres and destroying 169 homes. Ms. O’Conor, who is 53 and works as a public speaking coach and writer, drove back from vacation with her little dog, Nellie, a laptop, the clothes packed for traveling and a kayak, only to find that she had nothing else left. Her home, and everything in it, was incinerated, including those few heirlooms salvaged from the fire that destroyed her parents’ house in Glenview, Ill., when she was a child.

docs.abstract: Readers respond to the 2.20.11 issue.
docs.snippet: Readers respond to the 2.20.11 issue.
docs.lead_paragraph: Joshua Foer is right. In ancient times, memorization was a key skill vital to preserving knowledge. And it wasn’t only the ancient Greeks who used their memories in such a fashion. There are still vestiges of the vast bodies of knowledge that must have been common place in preliterate cultures. There are still a handful of Pacific Islanders who can navigate based on the precise position and distance of the stars above the horizon and on their knowledge of tides and currents. In many Muslim countries, it is commonplace for children no older than 10 or 12 to have memorized the entire Koran. Such feats of memorization are also common among Orthodox religious students and among Hindus who memorize chanted prayers and scriptures. Religion was once the major institution for passing on vital cultural knowledge. We are no longer lonely bands of hunter-gather warriors, so this vast amount of informationis no longer necessary. But the capacity is there, in all of us.RUANNEArkansas, Feb. 19, 2011, 9:56 a.m., nytimes.com

headline.main: The Memory Champion

docs.abstract: Everybody’s suddenly petrified about municipal debt. But the fate of bondholders ought to be the least of our worries.
docs.snippet: Everybody’s suddenly petrified about municipal debt. But the fate of bondholders ought to be the least of our worries.
docs.lead_paragraph: Vallejo, a city about 25 miles north of San Francisco, offers a sneak preview of what could be the latest version of economic disaster. When the foreclosure wave hit, local tax revenue evaporated. The city managers couldn’t make their budget and eliminated financing for the local museum, the symphony and the senior center. The city begged the public-employee unions for pay cuts — all to no avail. In May 2008, Vallejo filed for bankruptcy. The filing drew little national attention; most people were too busy watching banks fail to worry about cities. But while the banks have largely recovered, Vallejo is still in bankruptcy. The police force has shrunk from 153 officers to 92. Calls for any but the most serious crimes go unanswered. Residents who complain about prostitutes or vandals are told to fill out a form. Three of the city’s firehouses were closed. Last summer, a fire ravaged a house in one of the city’s better neighborhoods; one of the firetrucks came from another town, 15 miles away. Is this America’s future?

headline.main: Broke Town, U.S.A.
headline.print_headline: BROKE TOWN U.S.A.

docs.lead_paragraph: Believe it or not, Lady Gaga once had trouble getting any designers to lend her clothes. So much trouble in fact that she had her own knockoff-ish pieces made for the stage. That changed around the time Nicola Formichetti styled her for the September 2009 cover of V Magazine. She quickly owned the must-dress list. And now — as the muse for Formichetti’s new vision for Thierry Mugler — she’s come full circle. Let it be said, Gaga makes for a pretty sick model. Sometimes even the most captivating show can drag on, and rarely does the audience of editors walk out laughing about the good time they just had. Even the models appeared to be having a blast. The clothes — shiny and sexy, with sculptural shoulders sharp enough to be used as weapons — were fun too, and there’s nothing wrong with that.

docs.abstract: The first of the six space-adventure films that George Lucas and Industrial Light & Magic are currently converting for 3-D presentation will be released in theaters next year.
docs.snippet: The first of the six space-adventure films that George Lucas and Industrial Light & Magic are currently converting for 3-D presentation will be released in theaters next year.
docs.lead_paragraph: What will Darth Maul’s double-bladed light saber, Anakin Skywalker’s pod racer and Jar Jar Binks’s unyielding floppy ears look like to audiences as they appear to leap off the screen? And more important, when can they buy tickets for the first “Star Wars” movie to be released in 3-D? Lucasfilm and 20th Century Fox answered one of those questions on Thursday, announcing that “Star Wars: Episode I — The Phantom Menace,” the first of the six space-adventure films that George Lucas and Industrial Light & Magic are converting for 3-D presentation, will be released in theaters next year on Feb. 10. In a statement, the studios said the 3-D conversion is “being done with utmost respect for the source material, and with a keen eye for both technological considerations and artistic intentions.” (We assume that means artists won’t overemphasize the adorable chipmunk cheeks of a young Natalie Portman.) For science-fiction fans expecting to learn release dates for 3-D versions of the franchise’s other films (including the original trilogy of “Star Wars,” “The Empire Strikes Back” and “Return of the Jedi”), this isn’t the blog post you’re looking for.

headline.main: First 3-D ‘Star Wars’ Film Not So Far, Far Away: ‘Phantom Menace’ Coming Feb. 10

docs.abstract: A rock magazine that cares.
docs.snippet: A rock magazine that cares.
docs.lead_paragraph: After dinner last night, I ducked into that giant magazine store off Union Square, among the last of its kind. The lighting in there is as flattering as the full-body-cavity-search room at J.F.K. (not that I’ve been there), but it had the new April issue of Mojo on March 2, the sign of a newsstand that still cares. I rushed home and devoured the 17-page cover package on the Smiths, marking the 25th anniversary of “The Queen Is Dead” (which, interestingly, Mojo ranks as only their second-best album). Though it’s largely about the rock music of years gone by, Mojo steers clear of sentimentality and cheap nostalgia by sheer, unabashed devotion to its subject. Also: strong, well-defined sections, loads of vintage rock pictures, graphic design that draws inspiration from classic album covers and wonderful paper stock that feels so good in your hands.

headline.main: A Rock-Solid Magazine

docs.abstract: This week, The Moment features the artist Mike Kelley talking about Detroit, his hometown.
docs.snippet: This week, The Moment features the artist Mike Kelley talking about Detroit, his hometown.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are certain things that all creative people share in common — and lately a chat with the artist Doug Aitken seems to be one of them. Aitken’s 2006 book “Broken Screen,” which featured interviews with everyone from Robert Altman to Rem Koolhaas, challenged the convention of the linear narrative. Now, with his latest video project, Patterns & Repetitions [http://www.patternsandrepetition.com], the artist sits down with a whole new cast in an attempt to put the pieces of the creative puzzle back together again. There’s Jacques Herzog on instinct and architecture; LCD Soundsystem’s James Murphy on the sound of snow; and Jack White weighing in on Michelangelo as a modern-day blogger. This week, The Moment features the artist Mike Kelley talking about Detroit, his hometown. But don’t be fooled by the coffee mugs and the California sunshine. Aitken doesn’t do anything casually. The subtext of the conversations is nothing less than the future of art itself.

headline.main: Videophiles | Doug Aitken’s Patterns & Repetitions: Mike Kelley

docs.abstract: Madoff’s unsatisfying jailhouse remorse.
docs.snippet: Madoff’s unsatisfying jailhouse remorse.
docs.lead_paragraph: That’s what I’ve been wondering since catching up with Steve Fishman’s remarkable jailhouse interview with Bernie Madoff in New York Magazine. I’m not sure what I expected from the mastermind of a $65 billion Ponzi scheme, but it wasn’t whiny rationalizing like this: “Everyone was greedy. I just went along. It’s not an excuse.” Some crimes are so big that they demand full-throated, active voice, nonhedging remorse. (Not with “we participated” language a la Lloyd Blankfein, either.)  If only Madoff were more like Richard Nixon. True, it took hours of pushing and pressing by David Frost to get Nixon to apologize for Watergate — “I let the American people down, and I have to carry that burden with me for the rest of my life” — and he could have apologized for so much more. But watch Nixon’s face. Something is there. Could it be contrition?

headline.main: What Makes a Good Apology?

docs.lead_paragraph: Kate and Laura Mulleavy, the two Los Angeles-based designing sisters behind the fashion house Rodarte, have never had a solo exhibition on their home turf. Until now. “Rodarte: States of Matter,” which opens this weekend at the Museum of Contemporary Art’s Pacific Design Center gallery, treats visitors to an up-close look at 20 Rodarte creations, including six ballet tutus that the sisters designed for the film “Black Swan.” “We’re really happy to have the opportunity to show our work in an art museum,” Laura said. “We’re used to seeing our garments on tables in our studio as flat pieces that are kind of lifeless. For the exhibition, we wanted to abstract the clothes, removing them from the human figure, and show them as sculptural objects in the round.”

headline.main: Seeing Things | Rodarte’s States of Matter

docs.lead_paragraph: Fox trounced the competition in the ratings on Wednesday night as the dozen women remaining on “American Idol” took to the stage for a chance to advance to the reality show’s top 10. According to Nielsen’s estimates, 22.6 million viewers tuned in to Fox for the 90-minute episode, considerably more than any other show on the night. CBS ranked second with its back-to-back procedurals “Criminal Minds” at 9 p.m. (14.3 million) and “Criminal Minds: Suspect Behavior” at 10 (10.3 million). ABC placed third, earning solid ratings for “Modern Family” at 9 (10.1 million) but trailing at 9:30 with its new series “Mr. Sunshine” (7 million) behind Fox’s comedy “Traffic Light” (7.4 million). ABC’s 10 p.m. offering, “Off the Map,” struggled further with 5 million viewers. NBC was a distant fourth on the night, broadcasting a lineup of mostly reruns with the exception of a new episode of “Minute to Win It” at 9 (3.6 million).

docs.lead_paragraph: Contemporary British letters do not lack for memoirs, autobiographies and other works in which the main event is the father-son relationship. John Mortimer’s wonderful play “A Voyage Round My Father,” about his dad, a celebrated, blind barrister; Max Hastings’s funny and touching “Did You Really Shoot the Television?,” about his feckless but irresistible father; Auberon Waugh’s sublimely titled “Will This Do?,” about life with Evelyn, who comes off (to my mind, anyway) as the Dad From Hell; then there is Auberon’s own son Alexander’s superb multigenerational layer-cake memoir, featuring ­Auberon-Evelyn-Arthur; Martin Amis’s nuanced but adoring portrait of his dad, Kingsley; and most recently Christopher Hitchens’s brilliant “Hitch-22,” featuring his complex, fraught relationship with his father, Commander Hitchens of the Royal Navy. Rich terrain — and I’ve probably omitted a dozen or so others.

docs.lead_paragraph: The so-called floating population of China increased by 10 million last year, adding to the enormous number of people who are moving from China’s countryside to its cities to look for work, according to the National Population and Family Planning Commission. The total number of people who live in an area different from the one where they have a hukou, or permanent residence permit, is now 221 million, the commission said at a recent conference in Guangzhou, according to a report in China Daily on Thursday. Nearly 43 percent of that population was born after 1980 and nearly 75 percent are migrant workers. In the next three decades, another 300 million people from the countryside are expected to go to the cities looking for work. In recent years, senior Chinese officials have discussed reforming the hukou system so that migrants can get social welfare benefits available now only to those who have permits for the areas in which they live.

docs.abstract: With the means of its own destruction — nuclear weapons — humanity has itself to fear, Ron Rosenbaum cautions.
docs.snippet: With the means of its own destruction — nuclear weapons — humanity has itself to fear, Ron Rosenbaum cautions.
docs.lead_paragraph: Every thousand years a doomsday threatens. Early Christians believed the day of judgment was nigh. Medieval millenarians expected the world to end in 1000 A.D. These fatal termini would have required supernatural intervention; in the old days humans lacked sufficient means to destroy themselves. The discovery, in 1938, of how to release nuclear energy changed all that. Humankind acquired the means of its own destruction. Even were we to succeed in eliminating our weapons of doomsday — one subject of “How the End Begins” — we would still know how to build them. From our contemporary double millennium forward, the essential challenge confronting our species will remain how to avoid destroying the human world.

headline.main: Counting Down to Nuclear War

docs.abstract: “The novella is in its Golden Age as a form right now because no one is beating it with a stick until nickels fall out.”
docs.snippet: “The novella is in its Golden Age as a form right now because no one is beating it with a stick until nickels fall out.”
docs.lead_paragraph: “The only hope for a Golden Age, anymore, is being ignored. Bluntly, the novella is in its Golden Age as a form right now because no one is beating it with a stick until nickels fall out. So my plan for the novella is — drum roll: Do nothing. Or do whatever little is required to steward the status quo. Let’s agree, shall we, to keep throwing around the inane term Great American Novel, and to never, ever utter the phrase Great American Novella. Let’s agree not to remind California what it used to take for granted, that novellas, because of their length, can often be more handily adapted than novels into movies. Let us not remind New York what all the avid and demanding among us take for granted, that a volume of three novellas is more intriguing than one flabby novel. Let us downplay the novella in casual conversation. Writers, if you have a can’t-miss commercially viable yarn a-brewing, be good enough to stretch it into a short novel or compress it into a long story. And look, let’s keep the novella for ourselves, the adults. We deserve something, don’t we? Let’s free the novella of prizes and awards and citations and all manner of gold star. Let’s fail to educate our students about the novella, fail to convince them of its charms. That way, we need never be nostalgic for the Golden Age of the novella. We’ve got something they don’t want, a noncommodity, and we need to look out for it.”

headline.main: Block Quote: The Case for the Novella

docs.abstract: A penetrating interpretation of Edith Wharton’s “House of Mirth,” set in Newport Beach, Calif., during the bullish 1990s.
docs.snippet: A penetrating interpretation of Edith Wharton’s “House of Mirth,” set in Newport Beach, Calif., during the bullish 1990s.
docs.lead_paragraph: To take on a reinterpretation of one of the greatest novels of the 20th century in one’s debut is, to put it mildly, a gutsy move. Victoria Patterson’s first novel, “This Vacant Paradise,” set in Newport Beach, Calif., in the expansive, bullish 1990s, is a modern take on Edith Wharton’s “House of Mirth.” Patterson’s first book, a story collection, “Drift,” was also set in Newport Beach, but it concerned itself mainly with drifters, lowlifes and working stiffs rather than the upper crust.

Her opening, one of five winners, was appealing but not sensational. It moved swiftly from a couple of children lying in bed, listening as their father welcomes some visiting musicians downstairs, to a reclusive anatomist receiving news that a body has been found nearby, and back again to the children, eavesdropping on a conversation between their parents. A date and various details — a violoncello, a maid, the anatomist’s isolation from county society — established the setting as late-18th-century England.

docs.abstract: Weighed down by grief, the author makes a pilgrimage to Mount Kailas, venerated by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and others.
docs.snippet: Weighed down by grief, the author makes a pilgrimage to Mount Kailas, venerated by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and others.
docs.lead_paragraph: Trekking among the temples and monasteries of Nepal and southwestern Tibet, Colin Thubron hears variations of the same message whenever he consults a Buddhist priest: “The soul has no memory. The dead do not feel their past.” It’s not much consolation for an agnostic Englishman, aging and childless and now, after the death of his mother, the last surviving member of his family. But consolation — emotional if not intellectual or even spiritual — is what Thubron is after as he sets off on a grueling pilgrimage to the most sacred of the world’s mountains, an insurmountable eerie white cone that rises out of a barren plain in Tibet, shielded from easy access by the natural fortress of the Himalayas and the imported vigilance of the Chinese Army. Mount Kailas, the mystic Mount Meru of the Hindu scriptures, is venerated not only by Hindus but by Buddhists, Jains and practitioners of Bon, Tibet’s primeval faith. Together they constitute a fifth of mankind. Yet Thubron, approaching its inscrutable fastness, feels ever more solitary.

headline.main: Grief and Faith in Tibet

docs.snippet: Jacques d’Amboise recalls his decades with City Ballet — and Balanchine — as a tale of personal transformation.
docs.lead_paragraph: Since Jacques d’Amboise was among the most distinguished American male dancers of his day — his prime was probably 1952-74 — it is startling to read, in his memoirs, of his part in a stabbing. He had been a student at the School of American Ballet for several years when in the summer of 1949, heading home through Washington Heights in Manhattan, he found himself in a clash with a local bully, who produced a switchblade. “Without even thinking, I did a grand battement — a big kick — knocking his hand and sending the knife flying,” d’Amboise writes in “I Was a Dancer.” “The force of my kick spun me around on the ball of my foot 360 degrees. I arrived with both feet under me in plié, leaped in the air, and jumped so high my feet kicked down on top of his shoulders, smashing him to the ground.” Then d’Amboise, infected by “the virus of the bully,” pinned down his opponent, “stabbed him in the buttocks, tearing through his jeans, piercing the skin and drawing blood.”

Not a soul was inside the chapel-like storefront. I entered, stepped across a creaky wood floor, past a vitrine displaying antique wooden lasts, then ascended a narrow staircase along the back wall. Upstairs, in a kind of anteroom, there they were: exquisite shoes and boots, made by a family that has custom-shod royalty, celebrities and the very tasteful for nearly two centuries. docs.lead_paragraph: The composer Judd Greenstein’s music, beautifully wrought and consistently appealing, has not always seemed as audacious as his barnstorming initiatives with NOW Ensemble, the New Amsterdam record label and the Ecstatic Music Festival, all of which he helped to found. But “Sh’lomo” (“Solomon”), introduced during a festival program at Merkin Concert Hall on Thursday night, felt like an epiphany. Played by Mr. Greenstein’s new ensemble, the Yehudim, this work in progress fuses his disparate musical inspirations with his abiding interest in Jewish history and literature to explosive effect.

docs.abstract: A Rome court has sentenced a Catholic priest to 15 years in prison for sexually abusing minors, in one of the rare cases in Italy in which a bishop was called to testify in civil court.
docs.snippet: A Rome court has sentenced a Catholic priest to 15 years in prison for sexually abusing minors, in one of the rare cases in Italy in which a bishop was called to testify in civil court.
docs.lead_paragraph: A Rome court has sentenced a Catholic priest to 15 years and four months in prison for sexually abusing minors, in one of the rare cases in Italy in which a bishop was called to testify in civil court. The Rev. Ruggero Conti, from a parish in Rome, was found guilty on Thursday of abusing seven minors between 1998 and 2008, a lawyer for the priest said. The court also ordered Father Conti to pay 50,000 euros ($70,000) in damages to each victim. Father Conti was suspended from his duties as a parish priest in the outskirts of Rome soon after his arrest in 2008, but not from his clerical duties, said his lawyer, Patrizio Spinelli. He said his client would appeal the ruling.

headline.main: Italy: Priest Is Sentenced to Prison

docs.lead_paragraph: Queen Elizabeth is to make a state visit to the Irish Republic this year, the first by a British monarch in 100 years and the only one since Ireland broke from Britain to become an independent country. The visit, which will likely take place in early summer, is of huge symbolic importance and illustrates how far relations between Britain and Ireland have come since the struggles over independence and the worst days of the Troubles between the nationalists and unionists in Northern Ireland. Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, criticized the trip as “premature” but said that he respected the Irish president’s right to invite the queen to come.

docs.lead_paragraph: A strong sense of place runs through this cozy wine bar nestled amid a developing cluster of restaurants on Dyckman Street in Inwood. The proprietors, Benlly Polanco and his sister Dariana, have lived in the neighborhood since emigrating from the Dominican Republic in 1996 (or 1997, depending on who tells the story). The roughly 45 wines available were selected for their expression of terroir, said Vladimir Garcia, who used to work at the Chelsea Wine Vault and curated the list. The entertainment at Corcho Wine Room reflects the location, an evolving but strongly Hispanic neighborhood, with regular Latin jazz and conga nights, as well as wine classes and a harpist who plays pop and show tunes. The crowd, too, is decidedly local, and on Wednesday it included three friends catching up. DIANE CARDWELL

docs.abstract: Secession wasn’t evidence that the South didn’t have a reasoned intellectual life. In fact, it was the strongest evidence that it did.
docs.snippet: Secession wasn’t evidence that the South didn’t have a reasoned intellectual life. In fact, it was the strongest evidence that it did.
docs.lead_paragraph: Early 1861 found the 23-year-old Henry Adams in Washington, working as the private secretary to his father, Charles Francis Adams, a representative from Massachusetts. Adams was a keen observer even at that early age, and he focused much of his attention on the Southern political delegations going through the throes of secession. To Adams, the Southerners were little more than madmen. In a Jan. 8 letter to one of his brothers, he wrote, “I do not want to fight them … They are mad, mere maniacs, and I want to lock them up till they become sane; not kill them. I want to educate, humanize, and refine them, not send fire and sword among them.”

headline.main: The Minds of the South

docs.abstract: Johnson & Johnson said Friday that the president of its DePuy Orthopaedics division, a maker of artificial hips and knees that has struggled with product recalls and lawsuits, is leaving the company.
docs.snippet: Johnson & Johnson said Friday that the president of its DePuy Orthopaedics division, a maker of artificial hips and knees that has struggled with product recalls and lawsuits, is leaving the company.
docs.lead_paragraph: Johnson & Johnson said Friday that the worldwide president of its DePuy Orthopaedics division, a maker of artificial hips and knees that has struggled with product recalls and lawsuits over faulty implants, is leaving the company. The executive, David Floyd, submitted his resignation last week and will leave at the end of March, a spokeswoman said. He had been president of the unit since 2007. He is leaving to pursue interests outside the company, the spokesman, Lorie Gawreluk, said, declining to be more specific. DePuy recalled the ASR XL Acetabular hip system last August, after researchers found 13 percent of patients needed a repeat operation to fix problems with the implant. The company took a $280 million charge in the fourth quarter to pay for the recall. The company faces more than 500 lawsuits by patients who had the hip implants.

docs.abstract: In one of his most inspiring collections in a while, Junya Watanabe kept his familiar elements in perfect balance.
docs.snippet: In one of his most inspiring collections in a while, Junya Watanabe kept his familiar elements in perfect balance.
docs.lead_paragraph: Motorcycle jackets, couture shapes, tomboys — Junya Watanabe has explored all of these elements in the past. Today in Paris, though, they were in perfect balance in one of his most inspiring collections in a while. Mr. Watanabe didn’t overemphasize the 1950s hourglass shapes of his black leather jackets; he eased off the shape just enough to keep them contemporary. There were also capes and loose-back jackets, all in matte black leather that didn’t look rigid and wasn’t embellished. Another way he kept things contemporary was to put the molded jackets with A-line or softly gathered wool skirts that didn’t enhance your rear in a regrettable way. On the feet were updated jodhpur boots with moderately pointed toes.

headline.main: Junya Watanabe Takes Leather for a Ride

docs.abstract: The weekend box office was sturdy, at least at first glance.
docs.snippet: The weekend box office was sturdy, at least at first glance.
docs.lead_paragraph: The weekend box office was sturdy, at least at first glance. “Rango” (Paramount Pictures), left, an animated entry featuring the voice of Johnny Depp, was No. 1 in North America with about $38 million in ticket sales. “The Adjustment Bureau” (Universal Pictures) was second with an estimated $20.9 million, a good result for a difficult-to-market science-fiction thriller cum romance. Even the struggling CBS Films, exhibiting greatly improved marketing, had a decent weekend with its inexpensive “Beastly,” which sold about $10.1 million for third place. So was Hollywood in a glum mood? Moviegoers spent a total of $135 million on tickets over the weekend, a 31 percent decline from the same period a year ago, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box-office statistics. So far this year ticket revenue is down 20 percent on a 22 percent decline in attendance. The problem is that while films have been doing fine, there has been no blockbuster of the kind that can lift interest in moviegoing across the board. (Last year it was “Alice in Wonderland.”) Rounding out the top five were two holdovers; “Hall Pass” (Warner Brothers) sold about $9 million in tickets for a two-week total of $27 million, and “Gnomeo & Juliet” (Walt Disney) sold about $6.9 million for a four-week total of $83.7 million.

headline.main: ‘Rango’ Is Strong At Weak Box Office
headline.print_headline: ‘Rango’ Is Strong At Weak Box Office

docs.abstract: American Lyric Theater, an organization formed in 2005 to help develop new operatic works, has been chosen by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to receive a $90,000 grant.
docs.snippet: American Lyric Theater, an organization formed in 2005 to help develop new operatic works, has been chosen by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to receive a $90,000 grant.
docs.lead_paragraph: American Lyric Theater, an organization formed in 2005 to help develop new operatic works, has been chosen by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to receive a $90,000 grant. The money will be distributed to American Lyric over a three-year period to support its Composer Librettist Development Program, the group’s initiative to provide full-time mentorship to emerging opera writers through classes, workshops with professionals and residencies with New York City Opera. “No one else is doing this,” Mark Adamo, the director of professional development for American Lyric, said in a statement. “Aspiring librettists can study music-theater writing on the graduate level, but their work will draw overwhelmingly from the commercial and nonprofit theater, leaving unexamined the substantial differences that remain between the theater and the opera house.” “The Poe Project,” a series of three one-act operas inspired by the short stories of Edgar Allan Poe and written by six composers and librettists in American Lyric’s development program, had its first concert reading at Symphony Space in New York in November. The company is aiming for an official premiere in 2012.

headline.main: Grants for Opera Writers

docs.abstract: Dean Rader, an English professor at the University of San Francisco, has released his final list.
docs.snippet: Dean Rader, an English professor at the University of San Francisco, has released his final list.
docs.lead_paragraph: In February Dean Rader, an English professor at the University of San Francisco, set out to discover history’s 10 best poets (much like Anthony Tommasini of The New York Times recently did for composers). After spending two weeks compiling a list of nominees and fielding readers’ comments about them on the Web site of The San Francisco Chronicle, Mr. Rader has released his final list, with the Latin American poet Pablo Neruda at No. 1. “No poet has more passionately and thoroughly spoken for his people than Neruda,” Mr. Rader wrote, citing “Canto General,” a 15-part book comprising over 200 poems and 15,000 lines tracing the history of Latin America. “It is an insanely ambitious project that seemed to unify a country.” In second place was Shakespeare, whose name, according to Mr. Rader’s “shockingly unscientific measurements,” appeared most frequently in reader e-mails, followed by Dante, who Mr. Rader said was the most controversial pick, because “he’s only well known for one poem (‘The Divine Comedy’).” Western literary greats like Walt Whitman, John Donne, Emily Dickinson, William Butler Yeats and Wallace Stevens also appear on the list with the Eastern favorites Rumi and Li Po, whom Mr. Rader called “the great poet of drunkenness.”

docs.snippet: Not-so-good Takashi Miike films have zombies, sadomasochistic yakuza love stories, decapitated body parts turned into blood fire hoses, lengthy scenes of torture, and musical numbers. Good Miike movies have those things, too, though. An upcoming L...
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s prolific, and then there’s Takashi Miike. Since 1991, the Japanese director has made more than 80 feature films, plus some television, music videos and a kabuki drama. With that kind of work schedule, not all Miike films are going to be masterpieces. Not-so-good Miike films have zombies, sadomasochistic yakuza love stories, decapitated body parts turned into blood fire hoses, lengthy scenes of torture and musical numbers. Good Miike movies have those things, too, so it can be hard to tell which is which. For many fans, the difference is a matter of polish, but disagreements about whether more “polish” is desirable are frequent.

headline.main: Japan’s Splatter Auteur

docs.abstract: What can the plight of vase painters in Ancient Greece tell us about journalism now?
docs.snippet: What can the plight of vase painters in Ancient Greece tell us about journalism now?
docs.lead_paragraph: I didn’t know enough about Ancient Greece. I picked up a book published by Penguin that promised me, “the reader who is not a student or expert in classical literature,” the chance to be swept along “from the days of Mycenae to the splendors of Athens.” I would finally understand how Sophocles revolutionized dramatic history by introducing a third speaking actor. Never again would I mix up the “laughing philosopher” Democritus with democracy. Like any history book, the Penguin might help me comprehend our own history, in a vague way — they had slavery and freedom at the same time, too! But then I came to the plight of the vase painters, and I realized that I might as well be reading the Penguin Foretelling of the Fate of Newspapers in the Internet Age. Novelists, musicians, politicians and many others should also recognize themselves.

headline.main: Are We the Greek Vase Painters?

docs.lead_paragraph: Proving that it is possible for the star of a CBS comedy to take a break from his series without mortifying the network or his co-stars or burning all of his bridges in the entertainment industry, Jim Parsons, the “Big Bang Theory” star, will join the cast of the coming Broadway production of “The Normal Heart,” the play’s press representatives said Monday. Mr. Parsons, who in recent months has won an Emmy Award and a Golden Globe for his portrayal of the physicist Sheldon Cooper, will make his Broadway debut in “The Normal Heart,” playing Tommy Boatwright, a Southerner in a nascent group of HIV/AIDS activists in the early 1980s. docs.abstract: Pressure is growing in Washington for sterner measures against Libya, but a recent British adventure there suggests caution is in order.
docs.snippet: Pressure is growing in Washington for sterner measures against Libya, but a recent British adventure there suggests caution is in order.
docs.lead_paragraph: Senators John McCain and Mitch McConnell were out on the Sunday shows to push for more forceful American involvement in Libya. They were joined (with caveats) by an increasingly assertive Senator John Kerry, who insisted that a no-fly zone did not necessitate a military attack per se, contradicting Defense Secretary Gates’s statement on March 2. The question of American policy on intervention in Libya has been murky; Hillary Clinton seemed a bit more hawkish than the president for a while, as did Prime Minister David Cameron of Britain. Obama has been getting real results on Libya at the United Nations — in the Security Council, at the General Assembly and even in Geneva at the Human Rights Council. But in American politics, successes at the U.N. are not to be spoken of. Americans may have lost their taste for unilateral actions, but they haven’t gained one for multilateral actions either.Then how about some Special Forces sneaking about, as a sop to pride or at least an outlet for the national sense of adventure? Britain’s experience last week suggests caution is in order. A report in The Guardian this morning says a fellow named only Tom, whom the paper believes to be a British intelligence agent, had been working at the Al-Khadra Farm Company — which raises wheat southwest of Benghazi, Libya — for five months, until last Thursday, when he drove off into the desert at 3 a.m. with another foreign national, later returning with “large bags” and six armed Special Air Service men. Guards at the farm arrested them. That must have had a wilting effect on the S.A.S. men’s spirits. But farm personnel gave them a good hot breakfast and packed them off, and by Sunday the little band was safely away to Malta.

headline.main: Britain’s Excellent Libyan Adventure

The setting wasn’t a championship, however, but a regular-season game in the N.B.A., a loss by the home-team Miami Heat to the Chicago Bulls. We know this because the Heat’s coach, Erik Spoelstra, said so in his postgame comments: “This is painful for every single one of us to go through this, there are a couple of guys crying in the locker room right now, it is not a matter of want.” As you’d imagine, the general reaction hasn’t been one of extending gestures of comfort (for example). And you have to wonder what Spoelstra was thinking when he went all confessional, even if he didn’t name names — didn’t he learn anything from all that grief John Boehner recently had to put up with over his weepiness? As Spoelstra and the Heat are finding out, crying just doesn’t make for good “optics” most of the time. docs.lead_paragraph: Lincoln Center on Monday announced the third pillar of what is shaping up to be an especially high-profile festival this summer: the Mariinsky Ballet. The company will give eight performances at the Metropolitan Opera House in July, joining the Cleveland Orchestra and the Royal Shakespeare Company as major presences at the Lincoln Center Festival. The Mariinsky will present two works receiving their first United States performances, “Anna Karenina” and “The Little Humpbacked Horse,” full-length ballets choreographed by Alexei Ratmansky and set to the music of the contemporary Russian composer Rodion Shchedrin. A third program includes Alberto Alonso’s “Carmen Suite,” choreographed to Bizet’s music as arranged by Mr. Shchedrin, and “Symphony in C,” the George Balanchine work. Valery Gergiev, Mariinsky’s artistic director, will conduct.

docs.lead_paragraph: Constantinople is nominally a French-Canadian early-music trio, based in Montreal. But it is not quite that simple. It was founded in 1998 by Kiya Tabassian, an Iranian-born performer on the setar: a Persian lute with a long, rounded neck. The ensemble, which Mr. Tabassian directs, includes his brother, Ziya Tabassian, a percussionist who is particularly adept on the Persian tombak, a goblet-shaped drum, and Pierre-Yves Martel, a viola da gamba player who splits his time between Montreal and Paris. But the group seems rarely to work in this stripped-down form: its Web site lists a long roster of regular collaborators who play Middle Eastern stringed instruments and sing, as well as a flamenco guitarist, a clarinetist and a D.J.

docs.snippet: Alexei Ratmansky will choreograph a new version of the classic ballet “The Firebird” for American Ballet Theater.
docs.lead_paragraph: American Ballet Theater is no stranger to “The Firebird”: the troupe already has in its repertory several versions of the ballet set to Stravinsky’s 1910 score. But none of those were by its artist in residence, Alexei Ratmansky. That oversight is about to be rectified: Ballet Theater announced Monday that Mr. Ratmansky would be creating a new version, with scenery by Simon Pastukh and costumes by Galina Solovyeva, to have its premiere next March during the company’s Costa Mesa, Calif., engagement. New Yorkers will get to see the production during the spring 2012 season at the Metropolitan Opera House. For those keeping score at home, this will be Ballet Theater’s fourth production of “The Firebird” and the choreographer’s second — he created a version for the Royal Swedish Ballet in 2002.

headline.main: A New ‘Firebird’ for Ballet Theater

docs.snippet: Before the British-born Julian Imrie was a bootmaker, he had a peripatetic, romantic and unlikely life. We step into his shoes.
docs.lead_paragraph: Try to phone the British-born bootmaker Julian Imrie and you’ll probably get his voice mail, which begins: ‘‘I’m in the jungle right now.’’ Actually, on a recent weekday, Imrie, 39, was aboard a sailboat anchored somewhere in the French West Indies, when he was prompted, via e-mail, to recount his life thus far — a life that has been so peripatetic, romantic and unlikely that it’s almost obnoxious. Imrie quit college to assist Bruce Weber, went on to work on a horse farm in Montauk, N.Y., then movedto Amish country, where he salvaged crumbling barns. He spent a year studying the New Testament (in Greek). Then he biked from Los Angeles, his current home base, to Brazil. At one point, he decided to start Julian Boots, his stylish take on 19th-century footwear (from about $700, at Barneys New York), but first he learned how to make molds in the English Midlands and to tan leather in a 250-year-old Swiss factory. Now he’s an amateur boot historian, able to slip easily into a disquisition on what a 19th-century Cornish miner might wear. What his boots share with their fuss-free forebears, Imrie says, is that ‘‘you can use them in your garden and then rub them off and go to a wedding.’’

headline.main: Sole Mate

docs.lead_paragraph: The Long Wharf Theater of New Haven has lost its fourth managing director in less than a decade with the departure of Ray Cullom, whose resignation was accepted by its board, the theater said on Tuesday. Mr. Cullom came to the Long Wharf Theater, whose recent critically acclaimed productions include a revival of “The Glass Menagerie” starring Judith Ivey (which transferred Off Broadway to the Laura Pels Theater) and the American premiere of Simon Gray’s “Old Masters,” in May 2009 under what was supposed to be a five-year contract. But in a news release the theater said that Mr. Cullom was “leaving to pursue a professional opportunity in the producing and presenting theatrical world,” and that the board would soon announce a transitional management plan. Mary Pepe, chairwoman of the board, said in a statement that the theater was “very grateful to Ray for his leadership of Long Wharf during a period of unprecedented economic challenge.” Mr. Collum said in a statement that the theater “is an incredible place.”

headline.main: Managing Director of Long Wharf Theater Resigns

docs.lead_paragraph: The Akademie für Alte Musik Berlin is a magnificent chameleon of an ensemble. docs.abstract: Thirty years after his first show in Paris, the avant-garde designer is having his first exhibition in London, at the Victoria and Albert Museum.
docs.snippet: Thirty years after his first show in Paris, the avant-garde designer is having his first exhibition in London, at the Victoria and Albert Museum.
docs.lead_paragraph: In pursuit of imperfection, Yohji Yamamoto changed the course of fashion. Now, 30 years after his first show in Paris, which was greeted by astonishment, pro and con, the avant-garde designer is having his 30th museum exhibition, his first in London. The catalog that accompanies the show opening Saturday at the Victoria and Albert Museum (on view through July 10) reflects not just the heart-stopping beauty of the clothes, as photographed by Yamomoto’s longtime collaborators Nick Knight, Max Vadukul and Paolo Roversi, but also, in his own words, the designer’s enigmatic stance. So we learn, almost poignantly, that from the beginning: “I wanted to protect the clothing itself from fashion, and at the same time the woman’s body from something, maybe from men’s eyes or a cold wind.”

headline.main: Now Showing | Yohji Yamamoto

docs.abstract: What made Missouri different — and a central player in the lead up to the Civil War.
docs.snippet: What made Missouri different — and a central player in the lead up to the Civil War.
docs.lead_paragraph: Missouri was always different. Admitted to the Union under the Missouri Compromise, it was the eponymous exception to the agreement, which banned slavery north of the 36″30’ parallel — the line that defined the state’s southern border. And when, in November 1860, the northern free states voted for Abraham Lincoln, most slave states voted for John Breckinridge and three Upper South states voted for John Bell, Missouri was the only state to vote for the Northern Democrat, Stephen Douglas. The results in St. Louis were even more unusual: Lincoln edged out Douglas in a four-way race that — unlike any other that day — mirrored the returns of the country as a whole. St. Louis became the only large city in a slave state won by the president-elect, defying regional stereotypes. And Missouri stayed true to form on March 9, 1861, when its secession convention became the first such meeting to vote for staying in the Union.

headline.main: The Rise of the West

The arrest came as part of an investigation across Sweden and Britain into the bomber, Taimour Abdulwahab al-Abdaly, 28, who had lived in both countries and who detonated bombs in Stockholm on Dec. 11, 2010. The arrested man was described only as a “foreign national.”

docs.abstract: A look back at what people thought about looking forward, world-hunger-wise.
docs.snippet: A look back at what people thought about looking forward, world-hunger-wise.
docs.lead_paragraph: The particular challenges of feeding 9 billion people without destroying the planet seem both overwhelming and endlessly complex. Trying to peek into the future, however thrilling and terrifying it might be, is usually a failure. But it’s not, of course, unprecedented. (In fact, we’ve been here before, and in my adult-ish lifetime, too.) To that end I’ve been reading New York Times articles from the 1960’s (I was a teenager then) about food crises, and the challenge of feeding 6 or 7 billion people in the year (gulp) 2000. (I’m only permitted to link to the abstracts of these archived articles, but I’ll give you some highlights.)

headline.main: How the World Was Supposed to Look in 2000

docs.abstract: A new “peace movement” seeks to halt “the collateral damage” of the failed war on obesity.
docs.snippet: A new “peace movement” seeks to halt “the collateral damage” of the failed war on obesity.
docs.lead_paragraph: The start of Lent today will offer many of us yet another opportunity to renew that resolution we made at the start of the year (and abandoned by the time February rolled in), to lose the extra poundage. But before you vow to give up your glasses of Cabernet and your plates of pasta primavera, you might want to consider H.A.E.S., or Health at Every Size, a new “peace movement” that one of its proponents, Linda Bacon, a nutritionist in the Department of Nutrition at the University of California, Davis, says was designed to halt “the collateral damage” — food and body preoccupation, self-hatred and eating disorders — that has resulted from the failed war on obesity. H.A.E.S. is based on the idea that “the best way to improve health is to honor your body,” and it supports the adoption of good health habits simply for the sake of health and well-being rather than weight control.Bacon and Lucy Aphramor, a National Health Service specialist dietitian and an honorary research fellow at the Applied Research Center in Health and Lifestyle Interventions at Coventry University in England, published a paper in Nutrition Journal earlier this year. It argues that a weight-focused approach geared toward losing weight is — surprise! — not especially effective in either reducing the weight or creating healthier bodies. In fact, they say, such an approach can unintentionally lead to weight gain and worse health.

headline.main: Health at Every Size?

docs.snippet: The 26-year-old Columbia grad and founder of an exclusive beauty site, vensette.com, shares her list of favorite things.
docs.lead_paragraph: From first glance, Lauren Remington Platt appears to have it all. Statuesque, poised and intelligent, the 26-year-old looks more Westport, Conn., than West Village. Graduating from Columbia University in 2006, Platt became a research analyst at a hedge fund. Swapping out her Chanel jackets for chaos theory, long hours at the office left Platt only minutes and a mascara wand before hitting the benefit circuit post-work. This prompted the platinum-haired beauty to start Vênsette.com, a members-only Web site that allows its users to select from pre-styled hair and makeup options, starting at $250 for in-home visits by professional hair and makeup artists. Makeup options range from a natural, sun-kissed look to red-lipped Grace Kelly regalness, while hair styles run the gamut from a slicked-back ponytail (The Tribeca) to a classic, iron-straight middle part à la Gwyneth Paltrow at the Oscars. With an international gaggle of good-looking clients that include the model Anouk Lepere and Monaco royal Charlotte Casiraghi, who better than Platt to tell you how to put your best face forward.

headline.main: The Insider | Lauren Remington Platt

docs.lead_paragraph: The rap artist 50 Cent has made a donation to charity after revelations that he performed for the clan of Libyan leader Col. Muammar el-Qaddafi, Reuters reported on Thursday. “In light of the ongoing events in Libya, 50 Cent will be making a donation to UNICEF, which is providing vital relief supplies to meet the needs of women and children at risk during this crisis,” a spokesman for the artist told E! News. The rapper, whose real name is Curtis Jackson, joined what one entertainment Web site called the “Qaddafi performance regret club” – pop stars who sometimes earned seven-figure sums performing for members of Qaddafi’s family at exclusive parties around the world. These include Beyonce, Nelly Furtado, Mariah Carey and Usher, all of whom have issued statements saying they would donate or had already given money to charities. The appearances have become a major source of embarrassment since the Libyan leader’s brutal response to a popular uprising against him in Libya. 50 Cent earned an undisclosed amount from a private concert during the 2005 Venice film festival.

headline.main: 50 Cent Makes Charity Donation After Qaddafi Performance Revelation

docs.abstract: Eric Clapton raised $2.15 million at a New York auction of 75 guitars and 55 amplifiers on Wednesday, more than triple the pre-sale expectations.
docs.snippet: Eric Clapton raised $2.15 million at a New York auction of 75 guitars and 55 amplifiers on Wednesday, more than triple the pre-sale expectations.
docs.lead_paragraph: Social science was right: Eric Clapton raised $2.15 million at a New York auction of 75 guitars and 55 amplifiers on Wednesday, more than triple the pre-sale expectations, Reuters reported on Thursday. The proceeds from the sale at Bonhams – at which every lot sold — will go to the 65-year-old rock star’s Crossroads Center drug and alcohol treatment facility in the Caribbean. The auction – the proceeds of which totaled around $1.8 million without the buyer’s premium – also included instruments donated by Mr. Clapton’s musician friends Jeff Beck, J.J. Cale and Joe Bonamassa. Among the top lots was a 1948 Gibson L-5P, which was expected to bring $20,000 to $30,000 but raised $82,960; a 2005 Zemaitis S22BP 3S, estimated at $12,000 to $18,000, which sold for $75,640; and a pair of 1997 Fender Twin Amps, estimated at $9,000 to $12,000, which sold for $42,700. A team of Yale University psychologists studying people’s desire to own things once possessed by famous people recently concluded that “celebrity contagion” was the most important factor in such purchases.

headline.main: Eric Clapton Raises Money for Crossroads Center

docs.abstract: What can nomadic reindeer herders tell us about the cruelty of Soviet Communism?

docs.lead_paragraph: I am not sure I even realized that reindeer were real. I lost them decades ago along with Santa and his elves. I certainly did not know that reindeer and the people who herd them could tell me something new about the ridiculousness and cruelty of Soviet communism. But when I went to see a friend read from her novel earlier this week, she was paired with the English writer and polar nomad Sara Wheeler, who read from her latest book, “The Magnetic North: Notes from the Arctic Circle,” and I learned about the Chukchi people. The Chukchi are the “next door neighbors” from the very farthest northeastern section of Russia that Sarah Palin said she could see when she was the governor of Alaska. A local politician, Petr Omrynto, told Wheeler that “reindeer are the glue that binds Chukchi culture and society.”

headline.main: What Reindeer Herding Reveals About Communism

docs.lead_paragraph: With their political status still unclear back in their homeland, members of the Belarus Free Theater will be returning to New York next month for a five-week stay at La MaMa, which, along with the Public Theater, has offered the group an “artistic residency” as a gesture of solidarity. Beginning April 13, the troupe, which fled Belarus in December during a crackdown by the country’s authoritarian president, Aleksandr G. Lukashenko, will perform three of its original works, including the New York premiere of “Discover Love,” a meditation on marriage and political repression. Rounding out the program are “Being Harold Pinter” and “Zone of Silence,” both of which were critically praised when performed at the Public Theater’s Under the Radar Festival in January.

headline.main: Belarus Free Theater Returning to New York

docs.abstract: In this sprawling metropolis that anchors Brazil’s booming economy, the flaws — which include high prices and persistent drizzle — are no match for its teeming energy, which infuses everything from art to business to the city’s relentless night life.
docs.snippet: In this sprawling metropolis that anchors Brazil’s booming economy, the flaws — which include high prices and persistent drizzle — are no match for its teeming energy, which infuses everything from art to business to the city’s relentless night li...
docs.lead_paragraph: A CITY of high-rises and traffic jams in a country of rain forests and beaches, São Paulo, South America’s biggest metropolis, is a Brazilian freak of nature, except without the nature. But the city’s flaws — high prices, street crime, incessant drizzle — are no match for its strengths — artistic and business energy, relentless night life. Sometimes, it even manages to turn its flaws into assets, as when celebrated architects take ugly concrete and create post-Brutalist masterpieces, like Isay Weinfeld’s sleek bookstore Livraria da Vila on Alameda Lorena. São Paulo’s 11 million-plus inhabitants do their part by infusing the din with contagious Brazilian energy; those flashing smiles and thumbs-up signs are among the few things the city shares with the rest of the vast country whose booming economy it anchors.

headline.main: 36 Hours in São Paulo, Brazil

docs.lead_paragraph: Archaeologists are criticizing the Smithsonian Institution over a planned show of objects salvaged from a shipwreck in the Java Sea, saying that the company that recovered the objects did not observe professional archaeological standards in doing so, the Web site Science Now reported Thursday. The ship, a ninth-century Arab dhow that carried glazed ceramics and gold and silver vessels from China, was discovered in Indonesian waters in the late 1990s and salvaged by a German company called Seabed Explorations GbR. In 2005, according to Science Now, most of the objects were sold to a company in Singapore for a reported $32 million. (The exhibition is currently on display at the ArtScience Museum in Singapore.)

headline.main: Archaeologists Criticize Smithsonian Over Java Objects

docs.snippet: Cary Joji Fukunaga’s “Jane Eyre,” starring Mia Wasikowska, is a splendid example of how to tackle the daunting duty of turning a beloved work of classic literature into a movie.
docs.lead_paragraph: Jane Eyre may lack fortune and good looks — she is famously “small and plain” as well as “poor and obscure” — but as the heroine of a novel, she has everything. From the very first pages of Charlotte Brontë’s 1847 book, Jane embodies virtues that might be off-putting if they were not so persuasive, and if her story were not such a marvelous welter of grim suffering and smoldering passion. She is brave, humble, spirited and honest, the kind of person readers fall in love with and believe themselves to be in their innermost hearts, where literary sympathy lies.

docs.abstract: One thing you can say for sure about Picasso is that he never got stuck. A viewer-friendly exhibition at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, Richmond, captures his infectious fluidity over eight decades.
docs.snippet: One thing you can say for sure about Picasso is that he never got stuck. A viewer-friendly exhibition at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, Richmond, captures his infectious fluidity over eight decades.
docs.lead_paragraph: RICHMOND, Va.  One thing you can say for sure about Picasso is that he never got stuck. That is made beautifully clear by “Picasso: Masterpieces From the Musée National Picasso, Paris” at the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, Richmond. Selected by Anne Baldassari, chairwoman of the Paris museum, the exhibition’s 176 paintings, drawings, prints and sculptures give the impression of an artist in a constant state of creative flux and ferment from start to finish. He was nothing if not mercurial, and this viewer-friendly show captures his infectious fluidity over eight decades like no Picasso exhibition I have ever seen.

headline.main: What the Peripatetic Picasso Kept in His Closets

docs.abstract: Montaigne is often called the first blogger, but his skeptical moderation is in short supply in the blogosphere.
docs.snippet: Montaigne is often called the first blogger, but his skeptical moderation is in short supply in the blogosphere.
docs.lead_paragraph: Anyone who sets out to write an essay — for a school or college class, a magazine or even the book review section of a newspaper — owes something to Michel de Montaigne, though perhaps not much. Montaigne was a magistrate and landowner near Bordeaux who retired temporarily from public life in 1570 to spend more time with his library and to make a modest memento of his mind. He called his literary project “Essais,” meaning “attempts” or “trials,” and the term caught on in English after Francis Bacon, the British philosopher and statesman, used it for his own collection of short pieces in 1597.

headline.main: Montaigne’s Moment

docs.abstract: This week, The Moment features  LCD Soundsystem’s James Murphy on the sound of snow.
docs.snippet: This week, The Moment features  LCD Soundsystem’s James Murphy on the sound of snow.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are certain things that all creative people share in common — and lately a chat with the artist Doug Aitken seems to be one of them. Aitken’s 2006 book “Broken Screen,” which featured interviews with everyone from Robert Altman to Rem Koolhaas, challenged the convention of the linear narrative. Now, with his latest video project, Patterns & Repetitions, the artist sits down with a whole new cast in an attempt to put the pieces of the creative puzzle back together again. There’s Jacques Herzog on instinct and architecture; the artist Mike Kelley talking about Detroit, his hometown; and Jack White weighing in on Michelangelo as a modern-day blogger. This week, The Moment features LCD Soundsystem’s James Murphy on the sound of snow. But don’t be fooled by the coffee mugs and the California sunshine. Aitken doesn’t do anything casually. The subtext of the conversations is nothing less than the future of art itself.

docs.abstract: Chechnya’s strongman Ramzan Kadyrov is forcing women to observe an Islamic dress code, while the Kremlin remains silent, Human Rights Watch said Thursday.
docs.snippet: Chechnya’s strongman Ramzan Kadyrov is forcing women to observe an Islamic dress code, while the Kremlin remains silent, Human Rights Watch said Thursday.
docs.lead_paragraph: Chechnya’s strongman Ramzan Kadyrov is forcing women to observe an Islamic dress code, while the Kremlin remains silent, Human Rights Watch said Thursday. The New York-based organization said that women’s rights in the southern Russian republic had deteriorated to the point that they were not allowed to enter, much less work, in government offices without head scarves, long sleeves and skirts below the knee, and that girls and young women could not attend school or university if their heads were uncovered. Women are not allowed to enter movie theaters or concert halls or often even to be outdoors without head scarves, the Human Rights Watch report said. Tanya Lokshina, a Russia researcher at Human Rights Watch and the report’s author, said at a news conference in Moscow that the Chechen women shot with paintballs last summer for failing to follow the dress code were too frightened to file formal complaints. Some of the unidentified assailants were in uniform and thought to be law enforcement officials. Mr. Kadyrov has said that he was not behind the attacks, but that the assailants should receive awards for their deed.

headline.main: Chechnya: Women Forced to Wear Head Scarves, Report Says

docs.lead_paragraph: The police have discovered what they said was the largest cocaine processing lab ever found in Honduras, calling it a troubling sign of Mexican drug trafficking organizations spreading into their territory. The lab was found Wednesday on a remote coffee farm in mountains 100 miles north of Tegucigalpa after a six-month investigation with the assistance of the United States Drug Enforcement Agency, said Oscar Álvarez, the security minister. It was capable of producing about a ton of cocaine a month. Honduras is a growing transshipment point for cocaine from Colombia to the United States but Mr. Álvarez said the laboratory suggested the drug, usually processed in large clandestine laboratories in Colombia, was being refined in Honduras as well. Mr. Álvarez estimated the lab had been operating for the past two or three years. No arrests were made.

docs.lead_paragraph: A. O. SCOTT The movie world now finds itself in limbo between the Academy Awards and the summer movie season, which starts on the first Friday in May. These are the months of an annual mood swing from euphoria (or at least mild satisfaction) to despair (or at least mild dyspepsia). The Oscar broadcast may have been dreary and barren of surprise, but it did provide one last reminder that 2010 was, all in all, a good year for American movies. In the rearview mirror we have “Black Swan,” “The Social Network,” “True Grit,” “The Fighter” and “The King’s Speech”: all embraced by critics and popular with audiences. Up ahead we have more sequels than ever  “The Hangover ad Nauseam,” “Pirates of the Caribbean: Back for More of Your Money,” “X-Men Tiny Toons Adventure”  and thus a fresh set of reasons for critics and their readers to grouse about the horrible state of movies.

docs.abstract: As a solo artist, the Bay Area rapper has continued against the grain.
docs.snippet: As a solo artist, the Bay Area rapper has continued against the grain.
docs.lead_paragraph: Lil B first hit in 2006, at 16, when his group the Pack and its song “Vans” lionized the eponymous skate shoe that had, until then, most definitely not been associated with hip-hop style. (The song was unsponsored, akin to what Run D.M.C. did in the ’80s with their song “My Adidas.”) As a solo artist, the Bay Area rapper has continued against the grain. Last year’s album “Rain in England” melded ambient with rap, perhaps for the first time. A collaborative track with the goth-y Chicago/Michigan trio Salem in late 2010 demonstrated refreshing cross-genre (or subgenre) knowledge. Without being politically correct, Lil B is adept at playing clever word games to undermine some of the negative tropes inherent to hip-hop; his trademark boast — the constantly recycled lyric “I’m a pretty bitch” — uses egotism to unravel misogyny. In three years he has posted enough clips to his YouTube page — more than 240 songs, videos, remixes, video remakes and rambling commentaries — to create something of a canon. Those who explore it tend to grow obsessed.

headline.main: Lil B | Back to Cali

docs.abstract: Why hold it against Tiki Barber if some large part of the reason he wants to get back into the N.F.L. is to make money?
docs.snippet: Why hold it against Tiki Barber if some large part of the reason he wants to get back into the N.F.L. is to make money?
docs.lead_paragraph: You know that $9 billion in annual N.F.L. revenue we keep hearing about, that the owners and players are bickering over? Tiki Barber wants some of that. The former New York Giants running back, who quit after the 2006 season, has turned in his unretirement papers. The widespread assumption is that the soon-to-be-36-year-old, whose broadcasting career and marriage have both foundered badly, needs the money. And that’s a mercenary motive that makes some people mad, apparently, and some people sad. (If you’re John Riggins, age 63, it makes you want to throw on the old leather helmet again.) It also prompts one Mike to ask the other Mike on “Mike and Mike in the Morning,” on ESPN Radio, if it’s even possible for a football player like Barber to succeed in coming back if his primary motivation is money and not a raging love for the game. Mike (the former football-playing one) expresses doubt, says it would be hard. A coach in the N.F.L., Raheem Morris, who happens to coach Tiki’s twin brother, Ronde, says you have to have “the heart and the desire and the fire.”

headline.main: Retirement Play

docs.snippet: Slugging, if you don’t know – and I certainly didn’t before reading this great story – is a type of commuting practiced by suburbanites in Virginia traveling into Washington.
docs.lead_paragraph: Slugging, if you don’t know — and I certainly didn’t before reading this great Emily Badger article in Miller-McClune, thanks to commentary on it by Felix Salmon — is a type of commuting practiced by suburbanites in Virginia traveling into Washington. Those without a car wait in an orderly line and are picked up by those with a car who need extra passengers to take the speedy H.O.V. lanes. This has been going on for decades — an unplanned, unpaid, grassroots form of quasi public transportation that seems to benefit everyone. What particularly struck me was that, over time and without (apparently) any meetings or votes, everyone involved adopted a unique slugging etiquette.

headline.main: Transportation Etiquette

docs.lead_paragraph: On Thanksgiving 2008, Dana Adam Shapiro, a few years removed from his Oscar nomination for directing the documentary “Murderball,” visited his childhood home in Boston to find that a good friend of his was divorcing. The friend had been married for three years and, like Shapiro, was in his mid-30s. (Shapiro is now 37.) This was the fourth divorce that Shapiro heard about just that month. In fact, after absorbing the news, he sat down to make a list of all the couples he knew, under the age of 40, whose marriages had already broken up. He came up with 14 names. That struck Shapiro as too many. “It was unbelievable,” he says now. “I wanted to ask them all what went wrong, but you can’t ask those kind of personal questions of people. Unless you’re writing a book.”

docs.abstract: “Normally architects render a service. They implement what other people want. This is not what I do.”
docs.snippet: “Normally architects render a service. They implement what other people want. This is not what I do.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Over lunch in Los Angeles some months ago, with the actor Tobey Maguire and his wife, Jennifer Meyer, Peter Zumthor was imperious, charming and a little reserved, as usual. The Swiss architect was in town to discuss a new design for the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and Maguire and Meyer had invited him out to persuade him to build a house for them. Having long avoided commissions for houses for the rich and famous, Zumthor, now 67, lately concluded that it might be nice to put aside a little nest egg. Besides, he could imagine leaving a mark on a city where plenty of other great architects had worked. So when coffee arrived, he promised to take a look at the property but asked that Maguire and Meyer make a tour of his work in Europe and afterward visit him at his studio in Haldenstein to talk about what they saw. Then he would decide if he could design their house — whether, in effect, they could be his clients.

headline.main: The Ascension of Peter Zumthor

docs.lead_paragraph: Celebrate the local, and then the universal. That is how the Montreal Symphony Orchestra plans to mark the opening of its new concert hall in September. The orchestra late Thursday announced its inaugural concerts at the hall, which is due for completion this spring and has yet to be named. The opening program, to be performed Sept. 7, 9 and 10, will begin with works by three Québécois composers, Claude Vivier, Gilles Tremblay and Julien Bilodeau, and finish with Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9. The orchestra’s music director, Kent Nagano, will conduct. He will also lead a children’s concert as part of the opening festivities. The Borodin Quartet, the New York Philharmonic and the Mariinsky Orchestra are also scheduled to visit in the opening months.

headline.main: Montreal Symphony Orchestra Announces Inaugural Concerts at New Hall

docs.lead_paragraph: GNOMES AND UNKNOWNS: Thirty-five years ago, America was invaded by an army of tiny, ostensibly friendly eco-warriors in conical red hats. Their folkways were recounted in “Gnomes,” written by the Dutch doctor and children’s author Wil Huygen and illustrated with loving, Norman Rockwell-meets-J. R. R. Tolkien watercolors by Rien Poortvliet. The book sold more than a million copies and spent 56 weeks on the hardcover list before the little creatures crawled back under our collective Pet Rock. Now, an anniversary edition, published on April 1, aims to enlighten a new generation with its accounts of gnome biology (they weigh 300 grams and live an average of 400 years), gnome customs (they greet each other by rubbing noses and maintain friendly relations with rabbits) and gnome sex (which always results in twins, who live at home until age 100).

docs.abstract: The novelist Maxine Hong Kingston opts for poetry while taking a long look back in this 229-page free-verse memoir.
docs.snippet: The novelist Maxine Hong Kingston opts for poetry while taking a long look back in this 229-page free-verse memoir.
docs.lead_paragraph: Why would anyone want to be a poet? If that question seems too broad (or too harsh), let’s try a more modest one: Why would someone who’s already mastered an art form that is vastly more influential and lucrative than poetry — fiction or songwriting, for example — want to be a poet? The most famous poets aren’t famous, the richest poets aren’t rich, and not even the best-loved poets will ever enjoy the devotion inspired by Barbara Kingsolver, let alone Lady Gaga. So when a superstar from another arena turns his or her attention to poetry, the result can be like watching the Super Bowl M.V.P. forgo an entire season to devote himself to foosball. “Why,” one wonders, “is this person bothering?”

headline.main: Maxine Hong Kingston’s Life in Verse
