docs.lead_paragraph: It’s hard to think of another American chef who has outdone Gabrielle Hamilton in converting the humblest of stages into the heftiest of reputations. The restaurant she opened in downtown Manhattan in 1999, Prune, has barely enough room for the 30 diners it squeezes in at brunch, lunch and dinner, and despite the reliable presence of dozens of additional customers waiting on the sidewalk, she has either escaped or resisted the itch for expansion that so many of her contemporaries scratch and scratch. docs.lead_paragraph: Readers of his Op-Ed column in The New York Times know that David Brooks is an aficionado of research in the social sciences, especially psychology, and that he believes it has great practical importance. Now he has written a book, “The Social Animal,” in order to assemble the evidence for a certain conception of the human mind, the wellsprings of action and the causes of success and failure in life, and to draw implications for social policy. The book is really a moral and social tract, but Brooks has hung it on the life stories of two imaginary people, Harold and Erica, who are used to illustrate his theory in detail and to provide the occasion for countless references to the psychological literature and frequent disquisitions on human nature and society.

docs.lead_paragraph: About midway through Sharifa Rhodes-Pitts’s slim, enchanting volume we are introduced to rather an odd figure, L. S. Alexander Gumby, proprietor of the Gumby Book Studio and motive force behind a 1920s Harlem-based literary salon. The studio and salon both evolved, Rhodes-Pitts explains, out of Gumby’s singular passion for scrapbooking — his “impulse to compile, collect and curate the detritus of his reality.” Gumby’s efforts ultimately produced an apartment’s worth of materials about the so-called black experience, culminating, we are told, in a “brilliant and strange production.” These words well describe Rhodes-Pitts own achievement in “Harlem Is Nowhere.” Her happily disparate text blends the historical and the personal, the exceptional and the ordinary, adroitly communicating the multiplicity of Harlem itself.

docs.abstract: The controversial National Portrait Gallery exhibition “Hide/Seek,” which examined gay and lesbian themes in American portraiture, may come to the Brooklyn Museum and the Tacoma Art Museum, representatives of those institutions said.
docs.snippet: The controversial National Portrait Gallery exhibition “Hide/Seek,” which examined gay and lesbian themes in American portraiture, may come to the Brooklyn Museum and the Tacoma Art Museum, representatives of those institutions said.
docs.lead_paragraph: The controversial National Portrait Gallery exhibition “Hide/Seek” may come to the Brooklyn Museum, the museum’s spokeswoman, Sally Williams, said on Friday. The show, which examined gay and lesbian themes in American portraiture, won critical praise when it opened in October but later drew attacks from Republicans and religious conservatives over a video that included an image of ants crawling on a plastic crucifix. In response, the Smithsonian Institution removed the video from the show, prompting accusations of censorship and moving dozens of museums across the country to display the video and other works by the artist, David Wojnarowicz, in protest. “Hide/Seek” closed last month, but now the Brooklyn Museum and the Tacoma Art Museum in Washington State are collaborating to reconstitute it, Rock Hushka, the director of curatorial administration at the Tacoma museum, said. Mr. Hushka said that the planning was on a fast track, with an eye to the exhibition possibly opening in Brooklyn before the end of the year, and eventually going to Tacoma.

headline.main: Smithsonian’s Controversial Show May Come to Brooklyn Museum and Tacoma Art Museum

docs.lead_paragraph: The three owners of Klub Gastronomada wear two hats. The first has them as consulting food purveyors and growers in and around Croatia. But they also experiment with dishes in a sort of culinary laboratory; membership to the “Klub” gives regulars access to dinners with specially designed menus. But the restaurant proper, which opened in 2009, is open to all — though it helps to have an interest in the bounty of regional items that, through their consulting work, Gastronomada obtains from around southeastern Europe. Its 30 or so rotating menu items come from a stockpile of more than 250, which have been concocted in the laboratory.

docs.lead_paragraph: TOKYO — The first thing I was worried about was where to put my tea. I’d been sitting on the heated carpet in my apartment, working on a blog post about Japanese chewing gum. I stood up few seconds after the room started to sway. The TV was jumping. Buildings outside were swaying. A six-foot tall cabinet full of books was rocking. Things were falling in the kitchen and water was sloshing over the edge of the balcony, spilling from something above. I moved out from under the light fixtures and held onto a small table. I wanted to put down my tea cup, but there were no stable surfaces. Things were sliding around the floor.

docs.lead_paragraph: “American Idol” made its first elimination from its top 13 finalists on Thursday  Ashthon Jones  as Fox led the night with 21.7 million viewers, according to Nielsen’s estimates. The 8 p.m. episode lifted Fox to No. 1 on the night over all by a wide margin. CBS ranked second, winning the 9 p.m. hour with “CSI” (13.6 million), ahead of Fox’s “Bones” (10.9 million). At 8 and 8:30, CBS’s sitcoms “The Big Bang Theory” (12.1 million) and “Rules of Engagement” (9.5 million) remained solid, while at 10, CBS’s procedural “The Mentalist” dominated the time slot with 14.4 million viewers. ABC was third with a two-hour rerun of “Wipeout” from 8 to 10 (5.5 million), followed by a repeat of “Grey’s Anatomy” at 10 (3.5 million). NBC ranked a distant fourth with repeats of its comedy lineup.

docs.lead_paragraph: Franz Liszt had no special intentions for the musical sketches he made during his years in Switzerland in the 1830s. But many years and many revisions later, his little travel pieces had alchemized into a grand expression of his art: three suites for solo piano that he called “Années de Pèlerinage” (“Years of Pilgrimage”), the first based on Switzerland, the second on Italian art and poetry, and the third on introspective, spiritual concerns.

docs.lead_paragraph: For decades, Chinatown Fair welcomed everyone — misfits, cool kids, world champions, novices, dancers, fighters, strategists, tourists carrying leftover dumplings from their dinner across the street. Then, two weeks ago, it disappeared. Even among the devoted gamers and urban nostalgists who had been whispering about its demise for weeks, the end came as a surprise. About midnight, a simmering rent dispute forced Chinatown Fair, a video-game arcade at 8 Mott Street for several decades, to shut its doors; by the next evening it was stripped bare, an empty shell of a retail space with an old battered sign.

docs.abstract: Arguments in the more than three-year-long war crimes trial of Charles Taylor, the former Liberian president, ended Friday at a United Nations-backed court in The Hague.
docs.snippet: Arguments in the more than three-year-long war crimes trial of Charles Taylor, the former Liberian president, ended Friday at a United Nations-backed court in The Hague.
docs.lead_paragraph: Arguments in the more than three-year-long war crimes trial of Charles Taylor, the former Liberian president, ended Friday at a United Nations-backed court in The Hague. The case against the first African president to face an international tribunal has been the scene of much courtroom drama and multiple delays as the defense dragged out proceedings, ignoring deadlines and staging several boycotts. Mr. Taylor, 62, was indicted while in office in 2003 and charged with large-scale atrocities committed by rebels under his command. Mr. Taylor has denied the charges and dismissed his trial as a political event. If he is found guilty, he will serve his sentence in a British jail. The three international judges are expected to take months before delivering their verdict.

headline.main: The Netherlands: Taylor Trial Ends

Gilmer sent a rapid-fire sequence of letters to William Henry Seward, the new secretary of state. “I am here in the very midst of the South,” Gilmer implored Seward, “and I beg you to weigh well the suggestions which I make to you.” He described the nervous impetuousness among secessionists, who were beginning to believe that fighting and bloodshed were necessary to sustain their flagging revolution. Their only hope was to instigate a collision between federal and state forces in the Deep South.

docs.lead_paragraph: A judge ordered Friday that a Rwandan immigrant whose feeding tube was removed three weeks ago against her family’s wishes be given nutrition and hydration immediately. Rachel Nyirahabiyambere, 59, who has been in a vegetative state since suffering a major stroke, lay close to death in a Maryland nursing home early Friday, said her son, Jerome Ndayishimiye. Her family had felt powerless to save her after a court-appointed guardian ordered her feeding tube removed; the guardian, Andrea J. Sloan, believed that Ms. Nyirahabiyambere should be receiving only palliative care because she was “profoundly vegetative” and had no chance of recovery. After The New York Times published an article about her case, the Alliance Defense Fund, a Christian legal alliance, petitioned Judge Nolan B. Dawkins of Alexandria Circuit Court on behalf of her children. He ordered her feeding tube reinstated while the legal issues were weighed.

headline.main: Virginia: Judge Orders Nutrition for Immigrant in Nursing Home

docs.abstract: The Tomy Company, the Japanese maker of Transformers and Pokémon toys, agreed to buy the RC2 Corporation for $640 million to add Thomas the Tank Engine products in North America.
docs.snippet: The Tomy Company, the Japanese maker of Transformers and Pokémon toys, agreed to buy the RC2 Corporation for $640 million to add Thomas the Tank Engine products in North America.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Tomy Company, the Japanese maker of Transformers and Pokémon toys, agreed to buy the RC2 Corporation for $640 million to add Thomas the Tank Engine products in North America. The offer is valued at $27.90 a share in cash, 27 percent more than Wednesday’s closing price, the companies said. Tomy, based in Tokyo, is seeking overseas acquisitions to revive growth as falling birth rates in Japan, which contributed to two consecutive annual declines in revenue, crimps demand for new toys. In addition to Thomas, RC2 makes products under the Learning Curve, Johnny Lightning and Ertl brands. “This merger further enables Tomy to move towards our goal of increasing our global profile adding significant additional business in North America and Europe,” Tomy’s president, Kantaro Tomiyama, said in a statement. Shares of RC2, which is based in Oak Brook, Ill., rose $2.80, or 11 percent, to $28.31. Tomy’s stock rose 1 percent in Tokyo trading.

headline.main: Maker of Thomas the Tank Engine Toys to Be Acquired

docs.abstract: Valero Energy agreed on Friday to buy Chevron’s refinery in Pembroke, Wales, for $730 million and other related assets for about $1 billion.
docs.snippet: Valero Energy agreed on Friday to buy Chevron’s refinery in Pembroke, Wales, for $730 million and other related assets for about $1 billion.
docs.lead_paragraph: Valero Energy agreed on Friday to buy Chevron’s refinery in Pembroke, Wales, for $730 million and other related assets for about $1 billion. The transaction is the latest move by a big oil company to refocus on exploration instead of less lucrative refining operations. Chevron has already agreed to sell refining assets in more than 20 countries, and it is looking to sell more operations in the Caribbean and Central America. The deal also gives Valero, a major American oil refiner, its first significant foothold in Europe. The Pembroke refinery has a capacity of 270,000 barrels of oil a day, the vast majority of which is crude. Valero said it expected the purchase to immediately add to its earnings per share.

headline.main: Valero Agrees to Buy an Oil Refinery in Wales

docs.lead_paragraph: NEAR the entrance to “The Deconstructive Impulse,” at the Neuberger Museum of Art, is Lynn Hershman’s 1988 black-and-white photograph “Seduction.” In it, a woman vamps for the camera as she sprawls on a bed. She wears a short black dress and high heels, but instead of her head, a television set frames her oversize, mascara-heavy, closed eyes. docs.abstract: Largely forgotten, even by most Japanese, the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 was the worst calamity in Japan’s history.
docs.snippet: Largely forgotten, even by most Japanese, the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 was the worst calamity in Japan’s history.
docs.lead_paragraph: The earthquake hit in the early afternoon off the coast of Honshu, Japan’s most populous island, triggering unprecedented destruction. Ninety percent of the houses in a score of seaside towns collapsed in seconds. Passenger trains fell off railway bridges and plunged into the sea. A few minutes later, a 35-foot-high tsunami rolled in, sweeping away cars, houses and thousands of people, and burying entire towns in mud. Then came fires, fanned by winds and fueled by flimsy wooden houses, reducing much of what remained to ashes.

headline.main: In Deadly Earthquake, Echoes of 1923

docs.snippet: At Sunday night’s Olivier Awards, Britain’s equivalent to the Tony Awards, the Society of London Theater gave three prizes to “Legally Blonde, the Musical,” but none to Andrew Lloyd Webber.
docs.lead_paragraph: At Sunday night’s Olivier Awards, Britain’s equivalent to the Tony Awards, the Society of London Theater gave three prizes to the West End production of “Legally Blonde, the Musical,” but none to Andrew Lloyd Webber. “Legally Blonde” won best new musical, and two of its stars also took prizes, Sheridan Smith for best actress in a musical and Jill Halfpenny for best supporting actress in a musical. The award for best new play went to the Royal Court’s production of “Clybourne Park,” Bruce Norris’s political comedy about race relations in suburban America. (The play had a critically acclaimed run Off Broadway at Playwrights Horizons in 2010.) Other winners included Roger Allam for best actor, in “Henry IV, Parts 1 and 2” at Shakespeare’s Globe, and the actress Nancy Carroll for her turn in the World War II drama “After the Dance,” which won for best revival. The award for direction went to Howard Davies for “The White Guard,” which also took best lighting and set design. “Love Never Dies,” Mr. Lloyd Webber’s anticipated but poorly received sequel to “The Phantom of the Opera,” won nothing after receiving seven nominations in major categories. Stephen Sondheim was honored with a special award for his contributions to London theater.

headline.main: Olivier Awards Bypass Andrew Lloyd Webber

docs.abstract: “Mars Needs Moms” cost $150 million to make (excluding marketing) and managed to bring in only $6.8 million in North American ticket sales over the weekend.
docs.snippet: “Mars Needs Moms” cost $150 million to make (excluding marketing) and managed to bring in only $6.8 million in North American ticket sales over the weekend.
docs.lead_paragraph: The box office bomb Hall of Fame — “Ishtar,” “The Alamo,” “Cutthroat Island,” “Gigli,” “Speed Racer” — has a new member. “Mars Needs Moms” cost $150 million to make (excluding marketing) and managed to bring in only $6.8 million in North American ticket sales over the weekend. What happened? Unappealing alien characters, a tepid marketing campaign, family film gridlock at theaters and the movie’s antifeminist undertones contributed. But Hollywood will read this Walt Disney Studios flop as a rejection of Robert Zemeckis’s style of “performance-capture” animated filmmaking. (Mr. Zemeckis produced “Mars Needs Moms.”) Meanwhile a well-executed marketing push by Sony Pictures Entertainment catapulted “Battle: Los Angeles” to a stronger-than-expected No. 1 position over the weekend. This alien invasion movie had about $36 million in sales, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles ticketing data. The animated “Rango” (Paramount Pictures) held up in its second weekend, taking in about $23 million for a new total of $68.7 million and second place. “Red Riding Hood” (Warner Brothers) failed to tap into the “Twilight” fantasy fan base, selling a soft $14 million in third place. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a drama from Universal Pictures, was fourth in its second weekend, selling about $11.5 million for a new total of $38.5 million. “Mars Needs Moms” (a scene from the film, right) was fifth.

headline.main: ‘Mars Needs Moms’ ... and Paying Customers

docs.abstract: Riccardo Muti conducted the audience in a rare encore of “Va’ pensiero” during a production of Verdi’s “Nabucco” at Teatro dell’Opera in Rome on Saturday night, The Associated Press reported.
docs.snippet: Riccardo Muti conducted the audience in a rare encore of “Va’ pensiero” during a production of Verdi’s “Nabucco” at Teatro dell’Opera in Rome on Saturday night, The Associated Press reported.
docs.lead_paragraph: Riccardo Muti, below, conducted the audience in a rare encore of “Va’ pensiero” during a production of Verdi’s “Nabucco” at Teatro dell’Opera in Rome on Saturday night, The Associated Press reported. At the beginning of the show, Mr. Muti criticized the government for cutting Italy’s arts budget. When the crowd cheered for more after the chorus’s rendition of “Va’ pensiero,” Mr. Muti said he would allow an encore if the audience sang along in support of culture and patriotism. Less than five weeks after having heart surgery, and against the advice of his doctors, Mr. Muti was back at the podium on Saturday for the first of several performances of “Nabucco” planned for this month as part of Italy’s celebration of 150 years of national unity. “I don’t want, today, in 2011, that ‘Nabucco’ becomes a funeral hymn to culture and music,” Mr. Muti said before starting. He appeared energetic during the performance, according to The A.P., despite having had a pacemaker installed recently. In February, Mr. Muti fell from the podium during a rehearsal with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, of which he is the music director. He had what his doctor called “a common heart rhythm disturbance.” He is scheduled to conduct a concert performance of “Otello” in April at Carnegie Hall.

headline.main: Muti Leads Encore in Rome
headline.print_headline: Muti Leads Encore in Rome

docs.abstract: Fox is forgoing its planned preview this spring of “Terra Nova,” an ambitious drama involving time travel.
docs.snippet: Fox is forgoing its planned preview this spring of “Terra Nova,” an ambitious drama involving time travel.
docs.lead_paragraph: Fox is forgoing its planned preview this spring of “Terra Nova,” an ambitious drama involving time travel. The network said Friday that “Terra Nova” would have its premiere in the fall rather than in May, as it had been planned. The May premiere was intended to be a preview of the show, but the special effects will not be ready in time, Fox’s president of entertainment, Kevin Reilly, said in a statement. The visual effects are “essential,” he said, “so we are pushing back the special early preview date to give the visual effects team the time needed for their groundbreaking work.” The “Terra Nova” story starts in 2149, when Earth is dying and scientists must find a way to send a family back to a prehistoric, dinosaur-era version of the planet. docs.lead_paragraph: “Every Man Dies Alone,” a German novel about a husband and wife who oppose the Nazis in early 1940s Berlin, is about to be published there for second time, but with much more attention, the BBC News reported. The novel, by Hans Fallada, is based on the true story of Otto and Elise Hampel, who wrote anti-Hitler slogans on postcards and dropped them in public buildings. They were eventually arrested and executed. Fallada wrote the book soon after the war ended, when he was given the Hampels’ Gestapo file. The book was written quickly and had a quiet release in Germany in 1947, just after Fallada’s death. But it was not widely read until 2009, after its release in the United States and Britain. Aufbau publishing house in Berlin recently uncovered the unabridged manuscript and will publish a new edition, which is to include a deleted chapter depicting the Quangels, as the couple is called in the novel, as fans of Hitler until they learn of their son’s death on the German front. Penguin has said it is considering a release of the unabridged version in Britain.

headline.main: Novel of Wartime Berlin to Get a Fresh Life

docs.abstract: A handful of dazzling upgrades has made an island escape even more enticing.
docs.snippet: A handful of dazzling upgrades has made an island escape even more enticing.
docs.lead_paragraph: Development in the Caribbean tends to move on, well, island time. But this season, snowbirds were buzzing about a handful of dazzling upgrades. The biggest news is the re-launch of the Four Seasons Resort Nevis, which had been closed for two years following the destruction wrought by Hurricane Omar, which struck the twin island of Nevis and St. Kitts in October 2008. (The faltering economy played a role as well.) Now the resort on a prime stretch of Pinney’s Beach is back with a new design, a new spa director (who has come up with a new range of island-y treatments using rum, sugar cane and papaya) and a new chef, Andreas Donnerbauer, who will scuba dive with certified guests to pluck their supper right from the sea. The hotel has also added super-luxe day cabanas on the beach along with a sailing school. But guest favorites like the endangered sea turtle program and the Robert Trent Jones-designed golf course remain — as does Sunshine’s, the famous ramshackle bar just down the beach.

headline.main: Now Booking | Caribbean Face-Lifts

docs.lead_paragraph: Perhaps you are familiar with Meatpaper: Your Journal of Meat Culture. I was not, but how can anyone resist browsing such an attractive periodical? Especially when it’s called Meatpaper? Yet after flipping through the Spring 2011 issue for a a solid three or four minutes, I was still unsure: Is Meatpaper pro-meat? Is it an ironic dispatch from militant vegans? A pull quote under a movie still of Catherine Deneuve didn’t clarify matters: “The carcass comes to symbolize the psychosexual malaise by which Catherine Deneuve’s character is afflicted.” Well, sure — obviously. Which made me wonder whether Meatpaper wasn’t an anagram of ‘‘Meta Paper.’’ But regardless of its editorial mission, Meatpaper has surely published the definitive interview with Franc Fernandez, better known as the tailor of Lady Gaga’s meat dress:

docs.lead_paragraph: “That’s the beauty of the game.” It’s a useful phrase in sports talk. It allows you to sum up — without actually having to say much about — things like comebacks and buzzer-beaters and the unexpected twists and turns of unscripted athletic contests. But I’m going to use it as a way to characterize my reaction to two art installations I came upon the other day online. The first is a sculpture of Muhammad Ali … made up of speed bags … strung from wires. It’s very cool. (It’s probably also some sort of commentary on shifting perspectives and focus and, for all I know, maybe even various Greatest of All Time debates.) Even cooler is this installation connected to another G.O.A.T. candidate, the F1 racer Michael Schumacher. The pictures of his car, taken apart, each piece suspended from an art-gallery ceiling, are rather amazing. And now I’m going to call time on this post, before I start talking about things going down to the wire.

docs.abstract: A British jury ruled unanimously that Christopher Corbould, an Academy Award-winner for “Inception,” was not guilty of failing to ensure the safety of Conway Wickliffe, a cameraman killed in a stunt mishap on “The Dark Knight.”
docs.snippet: A British jury ruled unanimously that Christopher Corbould, an Academy Award-winner for “Inception,” was not guilty of failing to ensure the safety of Conway Wickliffe, a cameraman killed in a stunt mishap on “The Dark Knight.”
docs.lead_paragraph: A British jury said on Monday that an Academy Award-winning special effects coordinator was not responsible for the death of a cameraman who was killed in a stunt mishap during the filming of “The Dark Knight,” Reuters reported. After less than two hours of deliberation, jurors at Crown Court in Guildford, southwest of London, ruled unanimously that the effects coordinator, Christopher Corbould, was not guilty of failing to ensure the safety of the cameraman, Conway Wickliffe. Mr. Wickliffe was killed in 2007 on the set of “The Dark Knight,” Christopher Nolan‘s sequel to his superhero film “Batman Begins,” as he rode in a pickup truck driving parallel to a stunt car; the pickup missed a 90-degree turn and crashed into a tree. Last week, prosecutors argued that Mr. Corbould, who won an Oscar for his work on “Inception” and whose filmography includes several “James Bond” movies, did not follow proper safety guidelines in planning the stunt and that the accident was foreseeable. Mr. Wickliffe was honored in the closing credits of “The Dark Knight,” along with the actor Heath Ledger, who died before the film’s release.

headline.main: Effects Coordinator Cleared in Death of ‘Dark Knight’ Cameraman

docs.lead_paragraph: Several years ago, after having to drive for too long behind a truck full of stinking, squealing pigs being delivered for slaughter, I gave up eating meat. I’d been harboring a growing distaste for the ugliness that can be industrial agriculture, but the real issue was a long-suppressed sympathy for its — or really, my — victims. Even screaming, reeking pigs, or maybe especially screaming, reeking pigs, can evoke stark pity as they tumble along in a truck to their deaths.

docs.abstract: Trying to take in the scale of the destruction of the earthquake in Japan, I was reminded of what the great Japanese director Akira Kurosawa never forgot.
docs.snippet: Trying to take in the scale of the destruction of the earthquake in Japan, I was reminded of what the great Japanese director Akira Kurosawa never forgot.
docs.lead_paragraph: When the Great Kanto earthquake of 1923 and the fires that erupted along its trail destroyed Yokohama and three-fifths of Tokyo, killing nearly 150,000 people, Akira Kurosawa was in middle school. Kurosawa, the director of “Rashomon” and “The Seven Samurai,” never tried to put the wasteland that suddenly overtook the landscape of his childhood on film, but in interviews and an autobiography, he returned to the devastation again and again. Trying to take in the scale of the destruction in the aftermath of the earthquake last week in Japan, particularly the way active coastal towns were suddenly vaporized by the tsunami, I was reminded of what Kurosawa never forgot.

headline.main: Kurosawa on Earthquakes

docs.lead_paragraph: CBS’s procedural “CSI: Miami” and the reality show “Undercover Boss” delivered the most viewers in prime time on Sunday. According to Nielsen’s estimates, 11.8 million viewers tuned in to “CSI: Miami,” leading its 10 p.m. time slot and edging past “Undercover Boss” at 9 (11.7 million) to rank as the night’s most-watched show. CBS won the night easily, starting with “60 Minutes” in the 7 p.m. hour (10.3 million) and trailing only at 8 with “The Amazing Race” (9.4 million), which lagged behind ABC’s “Secret Millionaire” (11.3 million). ABC finished second even as it drew low ratings for repeats of “Desperate Housewives” at 9 (4.9 million) and “Brothers & Sisters” at 10 (3.2 million). NBC was third with 5.6 million at 7 for “Dateline,” 4.2 million at 8 at for “America’s Next Great Restaurant” and 8 million from 9 to 11 for “The Celebrity Apprentice.” Fox ranked fourth with its animated comedy lineup.

docs.lead_paragraph: Consider this: the most popular great Georgia rock band, the Allman Brothers, opened a 13-night stand on Thursday at the Beacon Theater on the Upper West Side. Three days later the least popular great Georgia rock band, Harvey Milk, opened its own three-night run at Union Pool in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. Both sang plenty of songs about suffering and dying; both were long-haired, guitar-heroic, deeply impressive. Both attracted sentimental audiences, somewhere in the 25-year span of middle age. The main difference between them was the size of those audiences. The Beacon theater seats 2,800; the Union Pool’s capacity is 74.

He had hidden on a wooded hillside and fired a high-powered rifle at officers responding to a call of possible larceny at a scrap yard in rural Buchanan County. The state police identified the dead officers as Cameron Justus, 41, and William Stiltner, 46. The wounded officers, who were both in critical condition on Monday, were Erik Rasnake, 32, and Shane Charles, 25.

docs.abstract: A GQ article on the fate of Mohammad Jawad, one of the two minors held for years in Guantánamo Bay.
docs.snippet: A GQ article on the fate of Mohammad Jawad, one of the two minors held for years in Guantánamo Bay.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the wake of President Obama’s announcement last week that military trials will resume at Guantánamo Bay and that the prison camp will remain open indefinitely, it’s well worth taking the time to read Michael Paterniti’s article from the February issue of GQ about the current life of former detainee Mohammad Jawad. Jawad is one of two minors (the other is Omar Khadr) held for years at the prison camp. His precise age is not known, but human rights workers and family members claim he was was 12 when he was detained in December 2002. (The American military says he was at least 16.) He was released from Gitmo in August 2009 after a federal judge ruled the military’s case against him was “riddled with holes” and the chief prosecutor of the case resigned in protest of the military commissions. Paterniti, who recently wrote about Haiti for this magazine, also compiled a partial but fascinating oral history of the camps, which accompanies his GQ article online.

headline.main: The Boy From Guantánamo

docs.snippet: The writer Ben Ryder Howe takes questions on his life post-deli and his relationship with his Korean mother-in-law, and even offers a few pointers on what to avoid at a convenience store.
docs.lead_paragraph: Imagine you’re an editor at The Paris Review, the product of a WASPy New England milieu. Your life entails daily interactions with George Plimpton — editing, writing, looking for the next Philip Roth. Then, for reasons that seemed reasonable at the time, you decide to pour your life savings into a cruddy bodega in the Boerum Hill neighborhood of Brooklyn for the sake of your Korean-American wife’s parents. A New York story par excellence, Ben Ryder Howe’s “My Korean Deli” is a hilarious account of clashing cultures and backbreaking, soul-squeezing vocational juggling. Here, Howe takes questions on his life post-deli and his relationship with his stubborn Korean mother-in-law (“the Mike Tyson of Korean grandmothers”), and even offers a few pointers on what to avoid at a convenience store.

headline.main: Now Reading | ‘My Korean Deli’

docs.snippet: Bob Dylan, whose songs like “Blowin’ in the Wind” and “Masters of War” were sung at many a Vietnam War-era protest, is scheduled to perform a set list of his own determining on April 10 in Ho Chi Minh City.
docs.lead_paragraph: That guy who said “The times they are a-changin’ ” really knew what he was talking about, didn’t he? Adding to the itinerary of locations where Bob Dylan has never previously played and where we never imagined he’d someday appear in concert, that ragged counterculture bard is slated to give a performance in Vietnam next month, The Associated Press reported. Mr. Dylan, whose songs like “Blowin’ in the Wind” and “Masters of War” were sung at many a Vietnam War-era protest, is scheduled to perform a set list of his own determining on April 10 at RMIT University in Ho Chi Minh City. Rod Quinton, the general manager of Saigon Sound System, a Ho Chi Minh City company that is promoting the concert, told The A.P. that Mr. Dylan “is a very important legend of music, and we think it’s important that Vietnamese people, particularly the younger generation, are exposed to his legacy and what he’s done for music.” The director of Art Performances Department of the Vietnamese government said Mr. Dylan had been granted permission to give the concert, which will come days after his first performances in China, in Beijing on April 6 and in Shanghai on April 8. The A.P. said tickets for Mr. Dylan’s Ho Chi Minh City performance would run from about $43 — just more than Vietnam’s monthly minimum wage — to about $120 for V.I.P. seats.

headline.main: Modern Times, Indeed: Dylan Plans First Concert in Vietnam

docs.snippet: Deborah Eisenberg was named the winner of the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction on Tuesday for “The Collected Stories of Deborah Eisenberg.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Deborah Eisenberg was named the winner of the PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction on Tuesday for “The Collected Stories of Deborah Eisenberg” (Picador), a compilation of four volumes of her work. It was chosen from a selection of roughly 320 novels and short story collections, all published in the United States in 2010. Laura Furman, one of the judges, said of Ms. Eisenberg’s collection, “From the first to the last of her collected stories, Deborah Eisenberg demonstrates her sharp intelligence, literary inventiveness and her clear understanding of human interconnectedness as it exists in isolation.” She will receive $15,000; the four finalists, Jennifer Egan, Jaimy Gordon, Eric Puchner and Brad Watson, will receive $5,000. An awards ceremony is scheduled for May 7 at the Folger Shakespeare Library in Washington.

headline.main: Deborah Eisenberg Wins PEN/Faulkner Award for Fiction

docs.abstract: A New York Times reporter was killed in World War II. The newspaper took awhile to explain what happened.
docs.snippet: A New York Times reporter was killed in World War II. The newspaper took awhile to explain what happened.
docs.lead_paragraph: Editor’s Note (slightly overdue). An article on Oct. 21, 1942, about the death of Byron Darnton, a war correspondent for The New York Times, described the death as “accidental” without any elaboration. Two subsequent articles said the boat he was traveling on “was bombed from the air.” It was many years before The Times explained further: Mr. Darnton was killed by friendly fire in an attack by an American B-25 bomber on the Australian fishing boat that was carrying the reporter and a force of American troops to Buna, in New Guinea. The circumstances of his death quickly became known to his family and were recounted correctly in Meyer Berger’s 1951 history, “The Story of The New York Times: 1851-1951,” and in a 1975 article in The Times by Martin Arnold reporting on the discovery of Mr. Darnton’s last notebook, the one in which he was writing when he died.

headline.main: All the News After 64 Years: The Story That Didn’t Fly

docs.snippet: Jordi Savall and his singers, dancers and musicians blend traditions and eras.
docs.lead_paragraph: Globalization has long had enemies along every point in the political spectrum, and colonialism, once considered a form of nationalistic virtue, is today regarded as an unalloyed evil. But in purely musical terms, there is a great deal to be said for hybrids born of different cultures coming into contact, and musicians grafting alien ideas about form, timbre, rhythm and harmony onto their own traditional styles. Yo-Yo Ma has made that point in his Silk Road Project, and Jordi Savall, the viola da gamba master and director of a handful of ensembles, has made a specialty of building programs from the fruits of musical cross-pollination and antique forms of multiculturalism.

docs.snippet: Last night, don’t ask me why, I plowed through the full 23-page transcript of Warren Buffet’s interview with the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission.
docs.lead_paragraph: Last night, don’t ask me why, I plowed through the full 23-page transcript of Warren Buffett’s interview with the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, discovered via Felix Salmon. It was surprisingly light reading; Buffett cracked himself up so many times there could’ve been a laugh track. He offered plenty of the plain-spoken discernment for which he is idolized — pricing power makes even an idiot C.E.O. look like a genius; investing in your house is a currency play (“really a way to go short on the dollar”); Wall Street profits by fooling its customers with complex risk underwriting (“There’s just more money in contracts that people don’t understand”); Bank of America’s Ken Lewis is the unheralded hero of the financial crisis because he saved the world as we know it by buying Merrill Lynch when he could have had it the next day for nothing.

headline.main: Warren Buffett’s Funny Take on the Financial Crisis

docs.lead_paragraph: I mentioned in my column that in recent weeks politicians in Florida and Iowa have introduced bills that aim to crack down on shooting photographs and videos of agricultural operations. The Florida bill would require anyone wishing to photograph a farm to first secure written permission from the owner. And what if they don’t? First-degree felony. The implicit goal here is to deter and criminalize damning undercover exposés like this one. The bill would also make it illegal for an agenda-less passerby to snap a picture of a farm from the side of the road, but my best guess is that those “crimes” might not be prosecuted quite so diligently.

docs.abstract: In which the ex-world champion learns to love the boring life.
docs.snippet: In which the ex-world champion learns to love the boring life.
docs.lead_paragraph: The gold caps on his teeth are gone, as are the frenzied trappings of celebrity: the nonstop partying, the cars, the jewelry, the pet tiger, the liters of Cristal. Mike Tyson — who was once addicted, by his own account, “to everything” — now lives in what might be described as a controlled environment of his own making, a clean, well-lighted but very clearly demarcated place. The 44-year-old ex-heavyweight champion is in bed by 8 and often up as early as 2 in the morning, at which point he takes a solitary walk around the gated compound in the Las Vegas suburb where he lives while listening to R&B on his iPod. Tyson then occupies himself with reading (he’s an avid student of history, philosophy and psychology), watching karate movies or taking care of his homing pigeons, who live in a coop in the garage, until 6, when his wife, Lakiha (known as Kiki), gets up. The two of them go to a spa nearby where they work out and often get a massage before settling into the daily routine of caring for a 2-year-old daughter, Milan, and a newborn son, Morocco; they also run Tyrannic, a production company they own. It is a willfully low-key life, one in which Tyson’s wilder impulses are held in check by his inner solid citizen.

headline.main: Mike Tyson Moves to the Suburbs
headline.print_headline:

LEARNED
TO LIVE
A BORING
LIFE.’

docs.lead_paragraph: The tragic bus crash last weekend that took the lives of 15 people heading home to New York after a day of gambling at the Mohegan Sun casino in Connecticut brought me back to Dec. 26, the day the blizzard of 2010 buried much of the East Coast in snow. My husband and I were flying home to New York City that day after visiting family in Cleveland for the holiday. When LaGuardia Airport was shut down just as our plane approached the city, the pilot announced that our flight was being diverted to the nearest available airport. We found ourselves in Syracuse — where it was not snowing! — wondering how, and when, we were going to get home. Eventually the airline gave the passengers who were on our flight the option of either checking into a hotel overnight or taking a bus to New York City, for those who were crazy enough to take their chances on the road.

docs.lead_paragraph: To help travelers avoid the pileup of indistinguishable black bags on the luggage carousel, Tumi has enlisted the graffiti artist John Matos to decorate a group of its lightweight Vapor cases. Matos, who goes by Crash, started spray-painting walls in the Bronx in 1975 and was showing in galleries and museums by the 1980s. For the Tumi project — which will be limited to 1,000 of each case in the four-piece collection — Matos explains that he “didn’t sit there thinking, What would be cool on a Tumi bag?” If he’d thought of himself as just a tagger for hire, he says, “the work wouldn’t have come out as good.” $445 to $595; tumi.com.

docs.lead_paragraph: AUSTIN, Tex. –The grand jury prize for the best narrative feature film at the South by Southwest festival went to “Natural Selection” on Tuesday night. The film, written and directed by Robbie Pickering, is a comedy about a woman who gets to know the eldest son of her husband, who has been a regular donor at a sperm bank. The grand jury prize for a documentary went to the director Tristan Patterson’s “Dragonslayer,” about the life and love of a youth in Fullerton, a Southern California suburb. “Natural Selection” also received prizes for performances by Rachael Harris and Matt O’Leary, and for its script, editing and score, setting it up as the big winner at a festival that focused heavily on low-budget films with small, personal stories. On Wednesday, by contrast, Jodie Foster was set to appear with “The Beaver,” from Summit Entertainment. That film, which she directed and in which she performs, stars Mel Gibson as a troubled toy executive who sorts out his life with the help of a beaver hand puppet. Mr. Gibson, who pleaded no contest on Friday to a misdemeanor count of battering his ex-girlfriend, Oksana Grigorieva, is not expected to attend the film’s Wednesday-night premiere. The South by Southwest festival, which explores, film, music and digital culture in presentations and panels, continues here through Sunday.

headline.main: ‘Natural Selection’ Wins Grand Jury Prize at SXSW

docs.abstract: The 60 short films in the 2011 festival were chosen from 2,862 submissions. They represent 20 countries and include 22 world premieres.
docs.snippet: The 60 short films in the 2011 festival were chosen from 2,862 submissions. They represent 20 countries and include 22 world premieres.
docs.lead_paragraph: They say there’s no such thing as a small role, but then what do you call a performance in a short film? The 60 short films selected for the 2011 Tribeca Film Festival include turns by actors as, well, big as Campbell Scott, Anthony LaPaglia and Colin Quinn. And some of the animated shorts feature the voices of David Duchovny, Joseph Fiennes and Ian McKellen. The films were chosen out of 2,862 submissions; they represent 20 countries and include 22 world premieres. Documentary subjects include a Haitian community that joins together to build a movie theater, a rock musician who decides to have transgender surgery, and a motivational speaker privately battling bipolar disorder. The narrative films include one in which a character tries to atone for a car accident that left a girl in a vegetative state; one about a man seeking justice after he thinks his son has been sexually assaulted; and — for those in search of lighter fare — a film titled “Mr. Stache” and described as “the awesome adventures of a man and his mustache.” The short films will compete for three awards — Best Narrative Short, Best Documentary Short and the Student Visionary Award — with combined cash and value-in-kind prizes totaling more than $15,000. The winner of Best Narrative Short will qualify for consideration in the short-film category of the Academy Awards without the standard theatrical run. The Tribeca Film Festival runs from April 20 to May 1.

headline.main: Tribeca Film Festival Selects Short Films

docs.snippet: The McCarter Theater’s 2011-12 season will include world premieres by  John Guare, Danai Gurira (“Eclipsed”), and the Irish playwright Marina Carr,  along with productions of Tom Stoppard’s “Travesties.”
docs.lead_paragraph: The 2011-12 season for the McCarter Theater in Princeton, N.J., will include world premieres by John Guare, Danai Gurira (“Eclipsed”), and the Irish playwright Marina Carr, along with productions of Tom Stoppard’s “Travesties” and a new musical directed by John Doyle and based on the songs of Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart, Playbill reported. The season will open with Mr. Doyle’s musical “Ten Cents a Dance,” a co-production with Williamstown Theater Festival, in which the cast doubles as the orchestra.  It will be followed by Ms. Carr’s “Phaedra,” an adaptation of that classical myth. Next up is “The Convert,” by Ms. Gurira, a playwright and actress who was one of the creators and stars of “In the Continuum,” about women living with AIDS in Africa and Los Angeles. “The Convert” is set in 1895 amid uprisings against colonialism in southern Africa. After “Travesties,” the season will close with Mr. Guare’s new play, “Are You There, McPhee?”

headline.main: New John Guare Play for McCarter Theater’s 2011-12 Season

In the distance the large salt lake Chott El Jerid shimmered in a brick-red mist. docs.lead_paragraph: Riccardo Muti, the Italian maestro and the music director of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, has been awarded the $1 million Birgit Nilsson Prize for his “extraordinary contributions” to the music world, The Associated Press reported. The prize was awarded by the Birgit Nilsson Foundation, established after the death of Nilsson, a renowned Wagnerian soprano, in 2005. The only previous winner, Placido Domingo, was chosen by Ms. Nilsson before her death; Mr. Muti was chosen, as subsequent winners will be, by the foundation and by a jury of at least five members. Mr. Muti, 69, who had surgery last month for facial injuries sustained in a fall from the podium during a rehearsal, was back at work last week conducting Giuseppe Verdi‘s “Nabucco” at the Teatro dell’Opera in Rome. Mr. Muti’s fall was related to fainting because of a heart rhythm disturbance;  he subsequently received a pacemaker.

headline.main: Riccardo Muti Awarded $1 Million Birgit Nilsson Prize

The same pattern applied to arrests for marijuana use.

docs.abstract: On why the average home cook should have a mandoline in their kitchen.
docs.snippet: On why the average home cook should have a mandoline in their kitchen.
docs.lead_paragraph: A mandoline seems to be one of the last frontiers for the home cook. Maybe it seems too fussy with all those different blades, or maybe people are under the impression that you have to buy the most expensive model, which can get extremely pricey. But even the cheapest mandoline will make your life so much easier in the kitchen. For example, while I could, with much time and a little effort, thinly slice the potatoes for a gratin (such as in my column on Wednesday), running them through a mandoline takes about three minutes and gives me perfectly even, gossamer slices, which melt into the cream while baking in the oven. I also rely on my mandoline for paper-thin slices of fennel and zucchini for salads, and lovely wafers of beets that I serve carpaccio-style with a walnut-mustard dressing on top. And then there’s my recipe for French apple tart, which depends on uniform slices of apple that are a breeze with a mandoline. So here are a few tips for those of you ready to take the plunge. Mandolines range in price based on the sharpness of the blade, the number of different cuts the blades will make and the sturdiness of the base.  I have used the Super Benriner (about $50), but years ago, I had the most basic Benriner ($20) and it served me just fine until the blades grew dull.  If you just want something basic, go for a cheaper model – they start somewhere around $15 (Norpro and Kyocera, for example, make them). And if you want something a bit more substantial (able to handle a more diverse range of fruits and vegetables), go for a sturdier, more advanced model. Oxo and Swissmar Borner (both about $40) are two reliable brands in this price range. And if you are looking to invest in something that will last you a lifetime and give you the widest variety of blades for different cuts, stainless steel professional models go for around $100, but you probably won’t ever have to replace them. Mandolines from MIU sell for about $110; Bron has one for $150 and De Buyer’s model, $229, allows for left-handed users. Most of the mandolines are compact and collapsible, which is particularly useful if you’re in a tiny kitchen and space is at a premium. And if you’re worried about cuts and scrapes, consider this glove, which has saved my knuckles from many an injury.

headline.main: Get Real and Get a Mandoline

docs.lead_paragraph: As the new minority party in the House, Democrats will need to keep their caucus together if they hope to win many votes. But in the early months of the 112th Congress, a clear pattern is emerging that could cause concern for party leaders: some House Democrats are voting against their party more often than ever. An analysis by The New York Times of the first 180 recorded votes in the House shows that 14 Democrats have agreed with a majority of their colleagues less than 70 percent of the time. docs.abstract: Gerald Wallace was a notable acquisition for the Trailblazers based on talent alone, but the more intriguing element of his arrival in Portland is the sheer number of lineup possibilities which his addition accommodates.
docs.snippet: Gerald Wallace was a notable acquisition for the Trailblazers based on talent alone, but the more intriguing element of his arrival in Portland is the sheer number of lineup possibilities which his addition accommodates.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s now clear that Gerald Wallace was only the most basic of the Portland Trailblazers’ trade deadline acquisitions. Simply, Portland added a former All-Star who plays tenacious defense, a valuable player on a decent contract who could obviously elevate the level of play from his spot in the rotation. However, dig deeper and what the Blazers netted was a ridiculous level of lineup versatility. With so many capable players able to swing between positions, Nate McMillan now has a canvas to handle all the free-form painting he can muster. McMillan has never been considered part of basketball’s avant garde, but he’s not afraid of going small, going big, or going with whatever works, and that makes him a worthy coach to handle such a strange roster.

headline.main: The Newest Element in McMillan’s Laboratory

docs.abstract: A revised version of the play, “Imagining Madoff” by Deborah Margolin, will open on Aug. 31 and run through Sept. 25.
docs.snippet: A revised version of the play, “Imagining Madoff” by Deborah Margolin, will open on Aug. 31 and run through Sept. 25.
docs.lead_paragraph: A play about Bernard Madoff that had been slated for production at a Jewish theater company in Washington last summer but was canceled after a legal threat from the author and Holocaust survivor Elie Wiesel, who was depicted as a character, will now go on at that theater in a revised version, The Washington City Paper reported. The play, “Imagining Madoff” by Deborah Margolin, originally depicted a close relationship between Mr. Madoff and Mr. Wiesel, who in real life lost all his and his wife’s savings and $15.2 million of his charitable foundation’s assets in Mr. Madoff’s Ponzi scheme. Before the play’s premiere at Theater J in Washington, Ms. Margolin sent Mr. Wiesel a copy of the script, hoping he would like it. Instead, he threatened to have his lawyer halt the production. Ms. Margolin agreed to revise the play, but when Theater J’s artistic director, Ari Roth, volunteered to show the revised script to Mr. Wiesel’s foundation, she decided to back out of the production entirely. Instead, she took the rewritten version — with Mr. Wiesel’s character replaced by a fictional Holocaust survivor and poet named Solomon Galkin — to Stageworks/Hudson, a small theater company in upstate New York, where it was performed last summer. Mr. Roth saw the play there and subsequently renewed a discussion with Ms. Margolin about producing it at Theater J. The play will open on Aug. 31 and run through Sept. 25.

headline.main: Fresh Life for Madoff Play in Washington

docs.lead_paragraph: Bahrain is a very little place — fewer than a million people on one modest island. But Bosnia was small too, and it helped kick off World War I. The risk in Bahrain is that battles there could ignite a broader Shiite-Sunni conflict. As Vali Nasr (currently at the State Department, in Richard Holbrooke’s old shop) wrote in his indispensable 2006 book, “The Shia Revival,” Bahrain’s Shiites, who account for more than 70 percent of the population, “consider themselves to be the salt of the earth ruled by a minority of Sunni settlers who invaded from Qatar in the eighteenth century.” Since Bahrain gained independence from Britain in 1970, Nasr writes, “Shias have been heavily involved in every coup attempt, street agitation, uprising and reform movement in the Persian Gulf emirate.”

docs.snippet: The 3-D film version of Michael Flatley’s popular stage show “Lord of the Dance” gives viewers this Irish dancing spectacle in an extra dimension.
docs.lead_paragraph: Presumably no one who doesn’t already love the clickety clickety clickety thump of Irish dancing is going to go to a concert film featuring an hour and a half of Irish dancing. And nobody who doesn’t already love the self-aggrandizing style of Michael Flatley is going to go to a movie focused relentlessly on Michael Flatley. So really only two questions need to be answered about “Lord of the Dance 3D,” a film version of Mr. Flatley’s popular stage show: Does whatever excitement this kind of spectacle holds transfer to film, and does the 3-D add anything?

docs.lead_paragraph: It should go without saying that Martha Graham is one of the greatest of all American artists and one of the great choreographers of all time. Twenty years after her death, however, fewer and fewer people have much grasp of her choreography. Graham herself outlived the larger part of her talent: almost none of her post-1960 works are worth watching seriously. Though the Martha Graham Dance Company guards the flame, most dancegoers under the age of 50 will have only sketchy ideas of her most famous works.

docs.lead_paragraph: A Tibetan monk in Sichuan Province tried committing suicide on Wednesday by setting himself on fire to protest Chinese rule in Tibetan areas, according to two Tibet advocacy groups, International Campaign for Tibet and Free Tibet, based outside China. The fate of the monk, Phuntsog, was unclear by nighttime, but there were rumors he had died. He was the second monk at Kirti Monastery to protest Chinese policies through self-immolation. In 2009, another monk did the same, but survived. This month is the third anniversary of an uprising against Chinese rule that rippled across Tibetan areas in March 2008. Kirti Monastery was a center of protests in Sichuan.

headline.main: China: Tibetan Monk Sets Himself on Fire

docs.lead_paragraph: It would seem that Sharron Angle is running for a House seat in Nevada. In a video on her Web site, Ms. Angle says she is “running for the United States Congress” but does not name the seat. Presumably it is the one in the Second District, which is being vacated by Representative Dean Heller, a Republican who narrowly defeated her in a 2006 primary run for the position. Mr. Heller is now running for the Senate seat left open by Senator John Ensign, the beleaguered senator who is not running again. Ms. Angle shook up her party and her state last year when she won the Republican primary and faced off with Senator Harry Reid, the majority leader, in a race she lost by several points. A messy primary could pave a path for a moderate Democrat in the district, which has been reliably Republican for decades.

headline.main: Nevada: Angle Announces She Is Running for Congress

docs.abstract: Moved by the plight of Japanese ceramicists, who have seen years’ worth of work destroyed in the recent earthquake and tsunami, three women in the U.S. have organized an auction to benefit their fellow artists.
docs.snippet: Moved by the plight of Japanese ceramicists, who have seen years’ worth of work destroyed in the recent earthquake and tsunami, three women in the U.S. have organized an auction to benefit their fellow artists.
docs.lead_paragraph: It has been almost one week since the devastating earthquake and tsunami struck Japan. If, like me, you love design, you probably have a favorite Japanese designer in fashion, architecture, graphic design or ceramics. Japan is a country that has always nurtured design, from handcraft to industrially produced goods; as a result, good design has become synonymous with Japanese design. Many of the country’s designers have been affected by the disaster, which continues to unfold in ways that are unfathomable to most of us. In Kasama and Mashiko, centers of ceramic production that are about halfway between Tokyo and Sendai, potters were hard hit by the quake when brick kilns collapsed and years’ worth of production shattered in minutes. Moved by the desire to support their fellow artists, three enterprising women in the United States have organized Handmade for Japan, an online auction of handmade work donated by Japanese artists and American artists with ties to Japan. Ayumi Horie, a Japanese-American potter who lives in Hudson, N.Y., recruited her friends Kathryn Pombriant Manzella and Ai Kanazawa Cheung to solicit donations and set up the auction, while the illustrator David Gordon designed a logo overnight. Offers of support, in-kind donations and handmade goods have poured in via Twitter, Facebook and e-mail. And artists including the illustrator Lisa Congdon, the textile designer Kaoru Oka and the ceramists Jun Kaneko, Justin Rothshank, Kathy Erteman and Diana Fayt, to name a few, have contributed paintings, shawls and, of course, pottery. The auction will go live on eBay on March 24 and will run through March 27. Through GlobalGiving, 100 percent of the auction proceeds will support relief efforts in Japan. To see more, check out Handmade for Japan’s Facebook page and Twitter feed.

headline.main: Seeing Things | Handmade for Japan

docs.abstract: Broadcasters there fear that lyrics in her song “Born This Way” are encouraging acceptance of homosexuality and may violate indecency laws.
docs.snippet: Broadcasters there fear that lyrics in her song “Born This Way” are encouraging acceptance of homosexuality and may violate indecency laws.
docs.lead_paragraph: You can’t read Lady Gaga‘s poker face, and you can’t hear her single “Born This Way” as the provocative pop singer intended on radio stations in Malaysia, where broadcasters are playing the song but obscuring lyrics that they feel encourage acceptance of homosexuality, The Associated Press reported. “Born This Way,” whose chorus proclaims “I’m beautiful in my way / ‘Cause God makes no mistakes,” would already seem a tough fit in Malaysia, where last year the singer Adam Lambert had a concert protested by the Pan Malaysian Islamic Party, which said his shows promote “gay culture.” And while radio stations there are playing the song, they have been garbling a lyric that says, “No matter gay, straight or bi, lesbian, transgendered life, I’m on the right track, baby,” for fear that it violates Malaysian indecency laws. The Malaysian broadcaster AMP Radio Networks told The A.P. that those lyrics “may be considered as offensive when viewed against Malaysia’s social and religious observances,” adding that being gay or bisexual is “still considered as a ‘taboo’ by general Malaysians.”

headline.main: Lady Gaga Gets Garbled on Malaysian Radio

docs.lead_paragraph: This week Home Fires is publishing “Still in the Fight,” a three-part series by the Marine combat artist Michael D. Fay, recounting his visit to McGuire Veterans Administration Hospital in Richmond, Va., where he spent two days with wounded Marines in rehabilitation. Fay, along with his fellow combat artist Richard Johnson, is a member of the International Society of War Artists (ISWA), and in co-operation with the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History’s Armed Forces History Division, set out to record a few days in the lives of wounded Marines in rehabilitation. In “Still in the Fight,” Fay offers both a written and visual account of time spent with three soldier and their families, on the mend.Though “Still in the Fight” deals with Marines wounded in Afghanistan, the series may be seen as a sequel to “Drawing Fire,” a five-part account published in 2010 that recounts in detail several weeks of Operation Steel Curtain in 2005 in Iraq. The conflicts in question are different, but both read in conjunction offer an inside view of the before, during and after of war.

docs.lead_paragraph: UNESCO is planning to send a delegation to Egypt early next week to assess the conditions at Egypt’s archaeological sites and monuments, Ahram Online reported. Egypt’s former antiquities minister, Zahi Hawass, was invited to attend a UNESCO seminar in Paris this week marking the 40th anniversary of the UNESCO convention that seeks to prevent the illicit trade of cultural property, but could not attend; instead, he sent a message asking the international community for help in finding objects that have been looted from Egypt’s museums and archaeological sites since that country’s revolution began in January. On Wednesday, Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities released an illustrated list of 54 objects missing from the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, which was looted on Jan. 28. docs.lead_paragraph: On a chilly night in the dead of a New England winter, Yasir Qadhi hurried down the stairs of Yale University’s religious-studies department, searching urgently for a place to make a private call. docs.snippet: A major collection of art, including props, costumes, backdrops and other objects used by  Merce Cunningham for dance performances will go to the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis.
docs.lead_paragraph: Even before Merce Cunningham died, in 2009, plans were being made to ensure the choreographer’s legacy. They included his company’s farewell tour, which comes to the Joyce next week, and a new box set of music composed for his dances. Now the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis has acquired a trove of material that major 20th-century artists like Robert Rauschenberg and Andy Warhol made for Cunningham performances. The collection covers some 150 props, costumes, backdrops and other objects. Among them are a Rauschenberg combine and his costumes for the 1958 dance “Antic Meet,” Frank Stella set pieces for “Scramble” (1967) and silver-colored pillows that Warhol contributed to “RainForest” (1968), as well as work by Jasper Johns. A spokesman for the museum would not comment on how much the Walker paid for the material. Some of the objects will go on display in November when the Merce Cunningham Dance Company’s Legacy Tour reaches Minneapolis.

headline.main: A Merce Cunningham Trove for the Walker Art Center

docs.snippet: Todd Eberle’s new book forces the reader to consider the visual kinship between disparate subjects.
docs.lead_paragraph: There is an almost clinical sobriety to the photos in Todd Eberle’s new book, “Empire of Space” (Rizzoli, $85). Culled from Eberle’s 30-year career and presented in pairs, the pictures force you to consider the visual kinship between disparate subjects: a Jeff Koons sculpture begins to look like a tomato; Granny’s plaid sofa becomes a Frank Lloyd Wright ceiling; and an old I.B.M. computer morphs into the United Nations Secretariat tower. Eberle says that after making this book, he finds such parallels everywhere: “It’s incredible to have a new way of seeing the world.”

headline.main: Seeing Double

docs.lead_paragraph: In 1949, the African-American painters Charles Alston and Hale Woodruff covered the lobby walls at a Los Angeles insurance company headquarters — a trapezoidal Moderne building designed by the African-American architect Paul Williams — with murals of early black Californians including explorers, cowboys and oil riggers. docs.abstract: That most cosmopolitan of metropolises, Hong Kong, is a city of contrasts, always reinventing itself.
docs.snippet: That most cosmopolitan of metropolises, Hong Kong, is a city of contrasts, always reinventing itself.
docs.lead_paragraph: IN Hong Kong, that most cosmopolitan of cities, contrasts abound. Ladies toting Gucci handbags wait two hours in dingy alleys for a coveted bowl of noodles. Incense-filled Buddhist temples fight for space with gleaming new high-rises. Cutting-edge art galleries share a block with junk shops. Always reinventing itself — a recent example being the rebirth of the former marine police headquarters as the 1881 Heritage, housing a luxury mall and boutique hotel — Hong Kong is a city of constant change. Its coiffed, work-hard-play-harder professionals attract the world’s most inventive chefs to their city, while the nonstop shoppers — soldiering on, late into the night — get first shot at the latest in fashion and design. Somehow, over seven million residents have managed to carve out a niche in this buzzing, compact, vertical city.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Hong Kong

docs.lead_paragraph: The Bolshoi Ballet, with a major tour to Paris planed for the spring and the opening of its theater set for the fall after a long renovation, is facing leadership turmoil. Its artistic director, Yuri Burlaka, left after his contract expired on Tuesday, according to Reuters, and no successor was named. Also on Tuesday, Gennady Yanin, the company director, abruptly resigned; on Wednesday, a 37-year-old Bolshoi soloist, Yan Godovsky, was named director in his place. News reports, referring to an article in the Russian daily Izvestia, said Mr. Yanin resigned after an e-mail with a link showing erotic pictures of someone who resembled him was sent to hundreds of people. docs.abstract: This week, The Moment features Jacques Herzog discussing instinct and architecture.
docs.snippet: This week, The Moment features Jacques Herzog discussing instinct and architecture.
docs.lead_paragraph: There are certain things that all creative people share in common — and lately a chat with the artist Doug Aitken seems to be one of them. Aitken’s 2006 book “Broken Screen,” which featured interviews with everyone from Robert Altman to Rem Koolhaas, challenged the convention of the linear narrative. Now, with his latest video project, Patterns & Repetitions, the artist sits down with a whole new cast in an attempt to put the pieces of the creative puzzle back together again. There’s LCD Soundsystem’s James Murphy on the sound of snow; the artist Mike Kelley talking about Detroit, his hometown; and Jack White weighing in on Michelangelo as a modern-day blogger. This week, The Moment features Jacques Herzog discussing instinct and architecture. But don’t be fooled by the coffee mugs and the California sunshine. Aitken doesn’t do anything casually. The subtext of the conversations is nothing less than the future of art itself.

docs.lead_paragraph: This is the second in a three-part series.Before leaving McGuire Veterans Administration Hospital, after our first day of sketching two battle wounded Marines, Richard Johnson and I go by the Wounded Warrior Detachment office and thank Gunnery Sgt. Alain Frederique for setting everything up for us. The “gunny” says there’s another Marine who would really love to participate, Lance Cpl. William “Kyle” Carpenter. It’s pretty late in the day, and we ask if we can set up a time to meet and draw him tomorrow. The Gunny tells us no — Carpenter will be at Walter Reed all of the next day for medical appointments. Carpenter’s face was virtually blown off and his right arm shattered by a grenade blast and after no less than 30 surgeries in nine weeks, he wants to tell his story. We don’t want to miss this opportunity.We find Lance Corporal Carpenter relaxing on his hospital room’s La-Z Boy lounger. His still-boyish face is a crazy quilt of scars. docs.abstract: Why velophilia is the closest thing London has to a political philosophy.
docs.snippet: Why velophilia is the closest thing London has to a political philosophy.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sitting astride a big, gray bicycle at the head of a long line of traffic on City Road last month, I studied the 20 or more other cyclists who were — with varying degrees of skill and impatience — crossing the intersection on a red light. Some were swerving among startled and cursing pedestrians, bells ringing; others had expertly timed a slalom between four lanes of cars. What all these cyclists shared, however, was a sense of liberating entitlement. For more than half a century, London’s historical tangle of streets has been owned by cars and vans and double-decker buses and black cabs. Not anymore.

headline.main: Boris Bikes Roll in London

docs.abstract: What James Franco, tiger moms and “Limitless” all tell us about the flaws of flawlessness.
docs.snippet: What James Franco, tiger moms and “Limitless” all tell us about the flaws of flawlessness.
docs.lead_paragraph: So, it’s the late fourth century, and you’re a British monk named Pelagius. You travel to Rome and are appalled by the low moral standards of the place. Maybe you’re stuffy, but you attribute the general air of laxity to Augustine, who believes man can attain perfection only through divine grace, not human effort. This just sounds to you like an excuse not to try. You believe free will means that we are free to make good choices — and that we should be severely punished if we don’t. So you track down Augustine in North Africa, where he tells you to take it easy. A guy can strive for perfection but can do only so much. Besides, it’s the effort that counts. But, of course, the argument doesn’t end there.

headline.main: Our Imperfect Search for Perfection

docs.lead_paragraph: Five years into his tenure, Justice Samuel Alito is the one conservative on the Supreme Court without a flashy legal signature. We know what to expect from the other justices on the court’s reliable right: Antonin Scalia has his constitutional theory of originalism, often in the company of Clarence Thomas. Chief Justice John Roberts also tends to lead with big legal principles. Alito usually reaches the same results as the others, but he does it by being small-bore. “He’s the offensive linesman on the team,” a clerk who worked for Alito when he was a federal judge says. “He puts his head down and stays focused on the case in front of him.”

docs.abstract: Is it difficult to remove a cracked bathroom-floor tile?
docs.snippet: Is it difficult to remove a cracked bathroom-floor tile?
docs.lead_paragraph: Is it difficult to remove a cracked bathroom-floor tile? DARDICK: You have to have a lot of patience. First you clean the grout around the tile with a sharp tool or diamond saw. Then you score the tile and break it up with a hammer. WAHAB: The hard part is when you are dealing with tiles that are installed close together, like marble. If the tiles are almost touching, it is very easy to break the adjacent tiles. It can be done, but it is riskier. SLOVAK: The critical thing is this: Do you still have that tile in that color in your house? Tile glazes change from lot to lot. That’s why when you are installing a new tile floor, you should buy extra tiles and leave them in your basement.

docs.abstract: Elvis Presley Enterprises is seeking “a work of art that symbolizes Elvis’ revolution in 1956.”
docs.snippet: Elvis Presley Enterprises is seeking “a work of art that symbolizes Elvis’ revolution in 1956.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Think of all that Elvis Presley has given you over the years: hours of memorable music; a couple of half-decent movies; the inspiration to decorate the jungle room of your home with floor-to-ceiling shag carpet. What could you possibly give the King in return as a key anniversary in his career approaches? Elvis Presley Enterprises, the company that manages that rock legend’s licensing, publishing and merchandising, is hoping it can entice you to create some Elvis-oriented art, in return for a shot at a Presley-themed prize package. To mark the 55 years since 1956, the fateful year when Presley released his single “Heartbreak Hotel,” his album “Elvis Presley” and his movie “Love Me Tender,” the company said in a news release that it is seeking a “a work of art that symbolizes Elvis’ revolution in 1956.” Entries can be provided in just about any medium (which would seem to include velvet paintings) and must be submitted in .jpeg or .pdf format at Elvis.com/revolution by April 28. The finalists will be chosen by a panel of judges, and the artist whose work received the most “likes” on Facebook (how very 1956!) will receive a prize package that includes a trip to Memphis, Tenn., during Elvis Week 2011; tickets to Cirque du Soleil‘s “Viva Elvis” show in Las Vegas; and a cabin on the 2012 Elvis Cruise (does it go to “Blue Hawaii”?). Any contestants who draw comparisons between Elvis Presley and Justin Bieber are disqualified in our book.

headline.main: Elvis Contest Seeks Elvis Art in Return for Elvis Prizes

docs.abstract: The seaside town of Margate, England looks to revive its fortunes with a new museum named for the painter J. M. W. Turner.
docs.snippet: The seaside town of Margate, England looks to revive its fortunes with a new museum named for the painter J. M. W. Turner.
docs.lead_paragraph: The seaside town of Margate, England, a thriving summer playground until its decline in the 1970s, is counting on the Turner Contemporary to revive its fortunes. Opening April 16, this striking museum — designed by David Chipperfield and named for the painter J. M. W. Turner, one of Margate’s famous visitors — has already spurred new galleries, pubs and cafes, as well as the restoration of Dreamland, a 1920s amusement park down the road. And it has inspired a lyrical new work by Tracey Emin, who grew up in Margate. Her pink neon sculpture “I Never Stopped Loving You” hangs adjacent to the museum. (Hundreds of people showed up to cheer its installation last year.) “There is more of an appetite for contemporary art here than you might imagine,” says Victoria Pomery, the Turner’s founding director. The inaugural show presents six artists whose works relate to a little-known Turner canvas depicting the Soufrière volcano on St. Vincent. “We want to help audiences get a better sense of the contemporary through the historical,” Pomery says. “And we will always have a Turner presence.” Adds Emin, “The other nice thing about the Turner is that it will have a really beautiful cafe, so people like my 82-year-old mum can go and look out at the sea and have a nice cup of tea.”

headline.main: Coast Garde

docs.snippet: Téa Obreht’s novel, “The Tiger’s Wife” is an unlikely best seller: a debut literary novel, set in the Balkans, that balances a war story against a collection of contemporary folk tales.
docs.lead_paragraph: BURNING BRIGHT: Its title might sound like a publicist’s dream mash-up of “The Paris Wife” (No. 8 on the hardcover fiction list) and “Battle Hymn of the Tiger Mother” (No. 11 on the hardcover nonfiction list), but Téa Obreht’s novel, “The Tiger’s Wife” (new at No. 11 on the hardcover fiction list), is in fact an unlikely best seller: a debut literary novel, set in the Balkans, that balances a war story against a collection of contemporary folk tales. Even before the book was reviewed on our cover a couple of weeks ago, keen readers may have been familiar with Obreht as the youngest member of The New Yorker’s “20 Under 40” coterie of fiction writers, announced last June when she was 24. (Other “20 Under 40” writers to make our best-seller lists include Joshua Ferris, Jonathan Safran Foer, Karen Russell and Gary Shteyngart.) Not that Obreht was unacquainted with best sellers before. In 2009, she wrote a post for The New Yorker’s blog The Book Bench in which she talked about her plans to read “Lolita” on a holiday flight to Russia. Distracted, she picked up her seatmate’s “Da Vinci Code” instead. “I doubt he cares that my copy of ‘Lolita’ wound up with him,” she wrote, “or that I finished ‘The Da Vinci Code’ three days later on a deckchair on our porch.”

docs.abstract: James Gleick argues that information is more than just the contents of our libraries and Web servers: human consciousness, life on earth, the cosmos — it’s bits all the way down.
docs.snippet: James Gleick argues that information is more than just the contents of our libraries and Web servers: human consciousness, life on earth, the cosmos — it’s bits all the way down.
docs.lead_paragraph: The universe, the 18th-century mathematician and philosopher Jean Le Rond d’Alembert said, “would only be one fact and one great truth for whoever knew how to embrace it from a single point of view.” James Gleick has such a perspective, and signals it in the first word of the title of his new book, “The Information,” using the definite article we usually reserve for totalities like the universe, the ether — and the Internet. Information, he argues, is more than just the contents of our overflowing libraries and Web servers. It is “the blood and the fuel, the vital principle” of the world. Human consciousness, society, life on earth, the cosmos — it’s bits all the way down.

docs.abstract: Charles Cumming’s thriller posits a sixth man among Britain’s notorious Cambridge spies.
docs.snippet: Charles Cumming’s thriller posits a sixth man among Britain’s notorious Cambridge spies.
docs.lead_paragraph: The five spies from Trinity College, Cambridge, may have betrayed their country during the cold war, but they performed an indisputable service for British literature. A number of works have either been inspired or enlivened by the misdeeds of Kim Philby, John Cairncross, Guy Burgess, Donald Maclean and Anthony Blunt. In Anthony Powell’s panoramic “Dance to the Music of Time,” for example, Lord Widmerpool gets into political hot water for what his wife derisively calls “his little under-the-counter Communist games.” Then there is the Irish writer John Banville’s elegant roman à clef, “The Untouchable,” which explored Blunt’s life. And novelists of such varying stripes as Ian Fleming and John le Carré have drawn sustenance from the treachery that emanated from 1930s Cambridge, where enlistment in the worker’s revolution seems to have easily accompanied sipping claret, participating in debauches and collecting Poussin paintings. After Burgess and Maclean, and later Philby, fled to Moscow, the K.G.B. must have sometimes wondered whether the information they supplied was worth the sheer bother of having to put up with these spoiled brats.

headline.main: A Thriller Revisits the Cambridge Spies
