docs.abstract: A physical and intellectual journey in search of undiluted moonlight.
docs.snippet: A physical and intellectual journey in search of undiluted moonlight.
docs.lead_paragraph: Moonlight beguiles, enchants and deceives. Like poems and dreams and love, it can be maddeningly difficult to characterize — some might say impossible. We know what it is, but we don’t know why it exerts such a powerful hold on the imagination, or how it works its magic. There’s a perfect madness in the desire to study moonlight, to wander across the world under its spell, to seek out the ways in which it alters reality, inspires art or otherwise leaves its mark on the soul. But that’s just the sort of intellectual wanderlust that seized James Attlee one evening during a walk on the coast of Cornwall as he watched “the rim of the harvest moon emerging from the sea, a monstrous, swollen apparition.” Struck by this spectacular sight, Attlee was also struck by the realization that our lives are no longer held, as they were “for countless millennia,” in the sway of the night sky. “Nocturne: A Journey in Search of Moonlight” is his eccentric, rambling, charming report “from this abandoned field,” a book by turns erratic and spellbinding.

headline.main: In Search of Moonlight

docs.lead_paragraph: In an era when publicity departments hotly compete with editors for space in the offices of financially challenged publishing houses, the old adage about how you shouldn’t judge a book by its cover is truer than ever. But what about titles? Surely it isn’t unreasonable to expect that a book with Jerusalem in its name — twice! — will be about . . . Jerusalem. But alas, James Carroll’s “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” is not really about that ancient city, and despite what its subtitle suggests, it has next to nothing to say about how Jerusalem “ignited our modern world.”

docs.snippet: The novelist Anne Roiphe examines her youthful compulsion to be a muse to “a man of great talent.”
docs.lead_paragraph: In her latest memoir, “Art and Madness,” the novelist Anne Roiphe, who married a playwright she mistook for a genius and sacrificed part of her youth to the god of self-deception, does not speak for all women who have married writers. Her darkly moralistic version of la vie bohème takes place in the 1950s and ’60s, not on scruffy Avenue B — where downtown artists tended to pride themselves on scraping along and being rejected by the Establishment — but on the fiercely status-conscious Upper East Side, only a short walk from Elaine’s. It is perfectly true, however, that both uptown and downtown, writers drank, womanized and had misogynistic attitudes. (Of course, so did the rest of America, which was running on alcohol after the war and was on the uneasy verge of a sexual revolution.)

docs.abstract: A exhibition featuring 650 red and white quilts, organized by the American Folk Art Museum, goes on view for six days from March 25.
docs.snippet: A exhibition featuring 650 red and white quilts, organized by the American Folk Art Museum, goes on view for six days from March 25.
docs.lead_paragraph: For six days only — March 25-30 — what promises to be an extraordinary exhibition will fill the Wade Thompson Drill Hall at the Park Avenue Armory. “Infinite Variety: Three Centuries of Red and White Quilts,” which was organized by the American Folk Art Museum, will present 650 red and white quilts — no two of which are alike — from the collection of Joanna S. Rose (who will donate 50 of them to the museum when the exhibition ends). The largest quilt exhibition ever mounted under one roof in New York City, it will fill the 55,000- square-foot drill hall to a height of 45 feet with a series of “rooms” defined by quilts that will be suspended on cardboard tubes. In the center of the installation, which was designed by the New York firm Thinc Design, a group of quilts will hang in a spiral formation that the designers liken to a tornado, above a circle of chairs that alludes to the social — and female-dominated — nature of quilting. Organized by Elizabeth V. Warren, a guest curator who is also a trustee of the museum, and Stacy C. Hollander, a senior curator at the museum, the exhibition will be free to the public and will include a cafe and shop. Even if you won’t be able to buy the quilts, the postcards should be terrific.

headline.main: Seeing Red (and White)

docs.lead_paragraph: IT was a Saturday night at Tony’s Bar in Nanjing, China, and as in any good university town, packs of rowdy students were making quick work of their pints. Young men bent low over tables playing boisterous dice games while their girlfriends, hair dyed various shades of red and brown, smoked disinterestedly and texted, their faces illuminated by the glow of their phones.

docs.snippet: The artist discusses his show “Walls, Diaries and Paintings,” now at Bryce Wolkowitz Gallery.
docs.lead_paragraph: A true flâneur, the artist José Parlá records his observations of the streets of cities like Havana, Istanbul, New York and Tokyo, collecting posters, taking photographs and writings on the wall, turning them into a visual diary. Consisting of memories written in calligraphic script layered on fragments of reconstructed city walls, Parlá’s paintings capture bits and pieces of his encounters. Born in Miami in 1973 to Cuban émigrés, and now a resident of Brooklyn, Parlá’s work has evolved into highly complex collages that emulate the various cityscapes he has visited. The Moment recently caught up with the artist to talk about his show “Walls, Diaries and Paintings,” which is at New York’s Bryce Wolkowitz Gallery until April 16.

headline.main: Asked & Answered | José Parlá

docs.lead_paragraph: THERE is a special kind of appeal to stories that lead us to the far boundary of the human and allow us a glance at what is on the other side, where the wild things are. What often comes into view out there is a projection of something buried deep within. That wolf in the bed, in grandma’s clothes, embodies some threatening animal emanation of the self, sexual or otherwise, lurking in disguise in our cozy domestic enclosures. Those invaders from outer space, preying on our cities, represent our own predatory, destructive urges in monstrous, alien form. And we can’t forget the vampires, whose cold glamour places them at the busy intersection of love and death, where our longings chase their morbid shadows.

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s fitting that in a film of “Appalachian Spring,” Isamu Noguchi is credited not with the set, but with the setting. He created the sparest of worlds. docs.snippet: The Mark Morris Dance Group performed three new works on Thursday night in its first production of the season at its home stage.
docs.lead_paragraph: Heart and brain keep meeting in the work of the choreographer Mark Morris, but each time with new results. Sometimes they marry in an irresistible outpouring whose meanings and structure reward further viewings. Sometimes they fuse in extraordinary dramatic poems buoyed by an underlying dance current. In either case we recognize him as one of the dazzling artists of our day. On other occasions they forge canny but tense alliances, with brain as the senior partner, drawing our attention to special feats of construction, nudging us to notice motifs and asking us to place meaning before pleasure. In a few works they simply collide, cancel each other out, or fight an unhappy duel to the death.

docs.lead_paragraph: A new food safety scandal erupted in China this week, this time over pigs in central Henan Province that were fed an illegal additive believed to speed up muscle growth and burn fat, resulting in leaner pork. The banned additive, clenbuterol, is considered hazardous to people and can cause nausea, headaches, limb tremors and cancer, the Chinese media reported. Authorities said they were investigating more than 1,300 pig farms. The police have detained more than 14 people and at least 6 government officials or employees have been fired or suspended, according to media reports on Friday.

docs.lead_paragraph: My sunday column looks at the way Japan has pulled together in the aftermath of its earthquake/tsunami/nuclear crisis and argues that we Americans could learn a thing or two from that reaction. The backdrop is the distress I’ve felt in the last few months as it has become apparent that in budget battles the tendency is to throw the weakest and most vulnerable sectors (i.e. children) overboard. In contrast, Japan seems to me to offer an example where stress knits a country more tightly together and where there has been a certain tendency for people to look after each other. docs.abstract: Lincoln and Henry Raymond, founder of The Times, helped each other weather the storm of disunion.
docs.snippet: Lincoln and Henry Raymond, founder of The Times, helped each other weather the storm of disunion.
docs.lead_paragraph: Students at the nerdier extremities of American history know that The Times was founded by Henry J. Raymond, a Republican stalwart of the 1850s, and they also know that the original Republican party — a fairly radical anti-slavery party — bears little in common with the modern GOP. But these early relationships are worth probing, for they show that The Times and Lincoln were helpful to each other on their way up, and that newspapers were anything but gray ladies as the conflict drew closer. It also shows that their symbiotic relationship was seriously strained in the weeks between the inaugural on March 4 and the outbreak of war on April 12. Like so many presidents since then, Lincoln found that The Times was getting on his nerves.

docs.lead_paragraph: The increasing star power of Bradley Cooper, right, helped lift “Limitless” to a stronger-than-expected $19 million in ticket sales over the weekend, easily making this supernatural thriller No. 1 at North American theaters. Produced for about $27 million, “Limitless,” about a writer who discovers a secret drug that gives him special powers, gives Relativity Media’s fledgling distribution operation a much-needed win. “Rango” (Paramount Pictures) was second with about $15.3 million in sales for a three-week total of $92.6 million, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box office data. “Battle: Los Angeles” (Sony Pictures Entertainment) was third with an estimated $14.6 million for a two-week total of $60.6 million. A much-publicized marketing partnership with Groupon.com appeared to be a failure for Lions Gate Entertainment, as its “Lincoln Lawyer,” produced for about $40 million, opened in fourth place with a tepid $13.4 million. “Paul,” a comedy from Universal Pictures that also cost about $40 million to make, was a disappointing fifth with $13.2 million.

headline.main: ‘Limitless’ and ‘Rango’ Lead the Way

docs.abstract: Russell Simmons and Ricky Martin were honored at the 22nd annual Glaad Media Awards presented by the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation.
docs.snippet: Russell Simmons and Ricky Martin were honored at the 22nd annual Glaad Media Awards presented by the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation.
docs.lead_paragraph: Russell Simmons and Ricky Martin were honored at the 22nd annual Glaad Media Awards presented by the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation on Saturday in New York. Mr. Simmons, right, a co-founder of Def Jam Records, a fashion designer and the author of several self-help books, received the award for excellence in media. Mr. Simmons recently took part in advertisements for the Human Rights Campaign, along with other celebrities, to support the New Yorkers for Marriage Equality campaign. Mr. Martin, who announced on his Web site last March that he is gay, was given the Vito Russo Award for promoting equal rights. Mr. Martin’s appearance on “The Oprah Winfrey Show” to talk about his experience also won for outstanding talk show episode. Other honorees included Frank Rich, former columnist for The New York Times; The Star-Ledger in Newark, for its coverage of the suicide of the Rutgers student Tyler Clementi; and CNN’s “Anderson Cooper 360” for an episode about the suicides of gay teenagers. The band the Scissor Sisters won for its album “Night Work” (Downtown Records), and Marvel Comics was recognized for its “X-Factor” comic series by Peter David. More awards will be announced later this year at ceremonies in Los Angeles and San Francisco.

headline.main: Glaad Awards for Russell Simmons and Others

docs.lead_paragraph: Two Canadian authors’ tales of youths growing up in isolation have been added to the list of nominees for the British Orange Prize for fiction written by women, BBC News reported. Emma Donoghue’s “Room,” which was also on the short list for last year’s Man Booker prize, made the cut of 20 writers, along with “Annabel,” the first novel by Kathleen Winter, a former writer for “Sesame Street,” about a young hermaphrodite growing up on the northeast coast of Canada in 1968. Ms. Winter joins eight other debut novelists on the list, including Téa Obreht, whose “Tiger’s Wife” was released to critical acclaim this month; Tishani Doshi (“The Pleasure Seekers”); and Samantha Hunt (“The Seas”). The short list of nominees will be announced on April 12, and the winner, who will receive almost $50,000 and a bronze statue, will be announced on June 8 at a ceremony in London.

docs.abstract: Sun Tzu’s dissection of military operations from more than 2,000 years ago will be turned into a graphic novel.
docs.snippet: Sun Tzu’s dissection of military operations from more than 2,000 years ago will be turned into a graphic novel.
docs.lead_paragraph: Next month “The Art of War,” Sun Tzu’s dissection of military operations from more than 2,000 years ago, will join the recent string of novels, television shows and, now, advice, business and motivational books to be turned into graphic novels. According to a report on the blog galleycat.com, the publishing group Round Table Companies, in partnership with Smarter Comics, will release a series of comic book adaptations of best-selling nonfiction titles. “The Art of War”; “The Long Tail,” by Chris Anderson; “From the Barrio to the Boardroom,” by Robert Renteria; and “How to Master the Art of Selling,” by Tom Hopkins, will be among the titles released in print on April 16 and as a free download online from April 1 through July 1. In an e-mail Corey Michael Blake, the chief executive of Round Table, said that he hoped to attract the interest of busy professionals, Twitter-generation readers who prefer to be entertained as they are educated, and traditional comic book readers. “I’ve been combining business and entertainment for years,” Mr. Blake wrote. “Seeing it working over and over, this was a gut play. My instinct told me that we had an opportunity to revolutionize the nonfiction reading experience.”

headline.main: ‘The Art of War,’ in Graphic Detail

docs.lead_paragraph: MAASTRICHT, the Netherlands — There are crowd pleasers at this year’s European Fine Art Fair, like a Rembrandt portrait regally displayed behind a black rope. There are also paintings by Renoir and Picasso, Miró and Warhol. But the main allure of this annual, super-size event is its breadth. docs.lead_paragraph: AUSTIN, Tex. — The keynote speech at the 25th annual South by Southwest Music festival, which took over downtown Austin from Wednesday to Saturday, was a bit grumpy. Bob Geldof, the Irish rocker who led the Boomtown Rats in the 1970s and went on to assemble the global Live Aid benefit concert in 1985 and its Live 8 sequel in 2005, bemoaned music’s loss of relevance. Although there was no shortage of “cool bands,” he said, music didn’t have the kind of broader social impact that it did with the Beatles, Bob Dylan, punk and grunge. He argued that music was no longer channeling rebelliousness and discontent.

docs.lead_paragraph: Emily Dickinson may have “dreaded that first robin so,” but she speaks for herself alone. To the rest of us, robins bring a mixture of joy and relief, the sign of a natural cycle still intact. The snow withdraws, and returning robins follow it across newly open ground like shorebirds tracing a falling tide. Their movement is almost as distinctive as their call: hasten and pause, hasten and pause. Once the ground is thoroughly thawed, there they are, tugging on earthworms as though they were the hawsers of the S.S. Earth.

But it wasn’t until he left his native Paris for Chile and translated his lyrics from French to Spanish that he and his career started to go places. After descending upon Los Angeles last year with a one-night-only Halloween Neckface show that drew 5,000 people, this weekend the two introduced the new L.A. home of their OHWOW gallery. Opening Saturday in a 4,000-square-foot, ivy-covered former Laundromat on La Cienega Boulevard in West Hollywood, OHWOW presented “Noblesse Oblige,” the first L.A. exhibition from Scott Campbell, who is as well known for the work he’s inked into the flesh of Marc Jacobs, Terry Richardson and others as he is for the intricate 3-D pieces he cuts into sheets of United States currency. “Noblesse Oblige” — an ironic battle cry for Campbell’s backwoods Louisiana kin and a phrase he has tattooed on his neck — also finds the artist working with neon, etching onto 24-karat gold plates, and drawing on the insides of ostrich eggs. We caught up with Bondaroff and Moran in the Rafael de Cardenas-designed space to discuss the bigger picture.

headline.main: Asked & Answered | OHWOW

docs.lead_paragraph: If, somehow, you have not heard of 13-year-old Rebecca Black, let me back up for a moment. docs.lead_paragraph: We all have an image of the politicians who started out in the log cabin or the farm and rose to greatness. It turns out this doesn’t happen very often. James Gimpel, Francis Lee and Rebecca Thorpe published a study in Political Geography finding that candidates and nominees for statewide office rarely come from rural parts of their states. Instead, these candidates and nominees come from the most populous counties—in numbers significantly out of proportion to these counties’ share of their state population. Gimpel, Lee and Thorpe argue that dense population fosters political ambition and provides candidates with the resources they need to pursue their ambition. The upshot is that rural areas are under-represented in state governments.

headline.main: Local Hero

docs.abstract: For every well-scratched washboard, there are too many awful renditions of “Amazing Grace.”
docs.snippet: For every well-scratched washboard, there are too many awful renditions of “Amazing Grace.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Sometimes, passing underground through Union Square or Times Square, you hear snatches of good music: the well-scratched washboard of the Ebony Hillbillies or the sonic eruption of the Hypnotic Brass Ensemble, who upset commuters boroughwide when they made the understandable if regrettable decision not long ago to move into the light. Riders are divided in their response to the single-minded intensity of Alice Tan Ridley, whose many renditions of “I Will Survive” are almost too authentic. Ridley, by the way, is Gabourey Sidibe’s mother (Sidibe played Precious in the movie of the same name a couple of years ago), and when the conversation turns to subway music, she is the first person many locals mention, rarely by name, almost always as “the woman who sings ‘I Will Survive’ for hours on end.” Ridley taught special ed before she hit the platforms, and after reaching the semifinals of “America’s Got Talent” last year, she has become perhaps our best-known subway performer.

docs.snippet: Seven years after the debut of her Indian-inspired jewelry collaboration with H. Stern, Diane von Furstenberg has added eight new pieces to the collection.
docs.lead_paragraph: Seven years after the debut of her Indian-inspired jewelry collaboration with H. Stern, Diane von Furstenberg has added eight new gem-inlaid yellow gold pieces to the Sutras collection. Rock crystals and diamonds are organically incorporated into the designs, using techniques employed by the Mughal Empire of Jaipur, India. “Gold embraces a gemstone and assumes its form,” says von Furstenberg of eye-catching pieces like the undulating teardrop crystal rings. “The movement within the gold alludes to sensuality and natural feminine forms.” Inspirational inscriptions, like love, laughter, harmony and freedom, are engraved on the back of each pendant, earring droplet and ring, a tribute to the power von Furstenberg sees in both words and gold. (Prices range from $3,200 to $8,200). “The combination not only adds beauty, but strength and empowerment as well,” she explains. Indeed, the collection displays a majestic embodiment of the literal translation of “sutra” from Sanskrit: a line that holds objects together.

headline.main: Sutras Stones | DVF and H. Stern

docs.lead_paragraph: Love and hate do battle in Charles Laughton‘s eerie 1955 film “The Night of the Hunter,” starring Robert Mitchum as a preacher harboring demons of his own. docs.abstract: Why the South moved its capital from Montgomery to Richmond, and what it meant for the War.
docs.snippet: Why the South moved its capital from Montgomery to Richmond, and what it meant for the War.
docs.lead_paragraph: The month of March, 1861, found the once sleepy riverside town of Montgomery, Ala., suddenly awake with the efforts to build the new Confederate government. Delegates from the seceding states had gathered there in February, and they had already written a constitution for the Confederate States of America and elected Jefferson Davis as president. Now the new Congress was busy with more routine matters like the postal service, liquor regulations and the salary of members. Cannons saluted arriving dignitaries and receptions, dinners and plays were regularly held. One delegate wrote his wife that “cheers, enthusiasm, and waving handkerchiefs” went along with “the work of bringing a nation into existence.”

headline.main: The South’s Capital Dilemma

docs.abstract: A New Orleans man pleaded no contest Monday to manslaughter charges in the killing of five teenagers in 2006, a case that shocked the city and then took a problematic path through the legal system.
docs.snippet: A New Orleans man pleaded no contest Monday to manslaughter charges in the killing of five teenagers in 2006, a case that shocked the city and then took a problematic path through the legal system.
docs.lead_paragraph: A New Orleans man pleaded no contest Monday to manslaughter charges in the killing of five teenagers in 2006. Michael Anderson, 24, was convicted of the murders in 2009 and was facing a death sentence. But a judge ordered a new trial after Mr. Anderson’s lawyers discovered that prosecutors had not turned over possibly exculpatory evidence. Before that new trial took place, Mr. Anderson was indicted on federal charges for his leadership role in a violent drug gang. He reached a deal with prosecutors, and pleaded guilty last Friday to helping plan a murder as well as to two other conspiracy charges. He also agreed to plead no contest to state charges of manslaughter in the 2006 killings, though, in his court filing, he maintains his innocence in that case. He faces a life sentence.

docs.lead_paragraph: An actor portraying Hamlet in an Irish production of that Shakespeare play sustained a palpable and frightening hit during a performance on Monday, resulting in his hospitalization, The Associated Press reported. Conor Madden, who is portraying the melancholy Danish prince in the Second Age Theater Company’s production of “Hamlet” being presented at the Everyman Palace Theater in Cork, Ireland, was wounded during a sword fight. The A.P. said that Mr. Madden sustained a cut beneath his eye and collapsed on stage, requiring the theater company’s artistic director, Alan Stanford, to go to the stage and explain to stunned audience members that this was not part of the play: the actor had been injured, and the play could not continue. Mr. Madden was treated and released. He will miss two performances scheduled for Tuesday but could return to the production as soon as Wednesday.

headline.main: Actor Is Injured in Irish Production of ‘Hamlet’

docs.abstract: What matter isn’t whether a war is multilateral, but whether it is wise.
docs.snippet: What matter isn’t whether a war is multilateral, but whether it is wise.
docs.lead_paragraph: Judging from my inbox, many readers interpreted this week’s column, which examines the perils inherent in the liberal interventionist style of warfare, as an implicit defense of the Bush administration’s rather different approach to the invasion of Iraq. (There were hints of a similar critique from Adam Serwer and Andrew Sullivan as well.) This was not my intention at all: As I’ve suggested before, I think that the Iraq War was a mistake in its conception and a botch in its execution, and I wouldn’t be supportive of our Libya intervention if it were being undertaken à la Rumsfeld (or John Bolton) rather than à la Samantha Power. My point, rather, was to push back against the conceit that the form of a war can vindicate its strategy — that what matters most in warfare is whether you’re “part of U.N. Security Council approved action” and whether the Arab League gives you the go-ahead, and that merely invoking the Obama White House’s multilateralism is sufficient to prove that our Libyan venture is far more responsible than the invasion of Iraq. Too many liberal Libya hawks (the president included) seem bent on persuading themselves that a strategically dubious intervention is justified so long as its goals are sufficiently high-minded and the French and the United Nations are on board. But the history of such interventions doesn’t bear their logic out.

headline.main: War Without Illusions

docs.snippet: Broken glass was found in the singer’s dressing room at “G.M.A.” after an interview in which the co-anchor Robin Roberts asked Mr. Brown about his relationship with Rihanna.
docs.lead_paragraph: After several months out of the spotlight, Chris Brown has the nation’s attention again, though surely not for the reason he intended. On Tuesday, the first day of release for his new album, “F.A.M.E.,” Mr. Brown reportedly left behind a dressing room strewn with broken glass at ABC’s “Good Morning America” after giving an uncomfortable interview to the “G.M.A.” co-anchor Robin Roberts. In the interview, Ms. Roberts asked Mr. Brown about a 2009 incident involving his ex-companion, the pop singer Rihanna, after which Mr. Brown pleaded guilty to a charge of felonious assault and was sentenced to five years of probation and six months of community labor. After Mr. Brown said that a restraining order against him had recently been relaxed, Ms. Roberts asked if he and Rihanna still saw each other; Mr. Brown replied, “I mean, not really,” and he avoided follow-up questions. Mr. Brown then performed a song from his new album and returned to his dressing room, where the “G.M.A.” morning staff members said they heard loud noises that prompted a call to security, according to a report on the ABC News Web site. It was later found that a window in the dressing room had been broken, leaving glass in the room and on the street outside ABC’s studio in Times Square, and that Mr. Brown and his representatives had left the building.

headline.main: An Uneasy Return for Chris Brown on ‘Good Morning America’

docs.lead_paragraph: There’s this story in Haruki Murakami’s “after the quake” (according to Jay Rubin, the book’s translator, Murakami insisted that the title be lowercase) called “Super-Frog Saves Tokyo.” The book is a collection of short stories about the psychic aftershocks of the ’95 Kobe earthquake. (Here’s a fascinating conversation between Murakami and Jonathan Lethem, plus audio of Murakami reading “Super-Frog.”) Five of the six stories are more or less straight-up realism, but “Super-Frog” is from the land of Kafka. A slightly overwhelmed and depressive banker named Katagiri comes home one day to find a huge Dostoyevsky-quoting frog in his house. The frog tells Katagiri that he needs his help defeating the monstrous Worm that’s raging beneath the streets of Tokyo. (Worm, by the way, is a version of the catfish of Japanese mythology, which my colleague Harvey Dickson wrote about.)

headline.main: Super-Frog

docs.abstract: Hammond Dairy in the Hudson Valley specializes in yogurt that can go from breakfast to dessert.
docs.snippet: Hammond Dairy in the Hudson Valley specializes in yogurt that can go from breakfast to dessert.
docs.lead_paragraph: Hammond Dairy in Amenia, N.Y., in the Hudson Valley, specializes in yogurt that can go from breakfast to dessert. It’s unhomogenized whole milk yogurt with a gentle flavor, even though it’s made with five kinds of active cultures. In addition to the delicious plain, which can enhance a bowl of granola in the morning, there is a richer vanilla, and three fruit flavors: strawberry, raspberry and peach, all made with local fruit (not Hammond’s own). For that dessert there is chocolate, best enjoyed by inverting the contents into a dish so the chocolate sauce, which is on the bottom, becomes a sundaelike topping for what amounts to a panna cotta for health nuts. You can serve the fruit yogurts this way, too.

headline.main: Yogurt to Start the Morning or End the Day

docs.abstract: Hangar One’s chipotle vodka, made with several kinds of fresh, dried and smoked chilies, is now in stores across the country.
docs.snippet: Hangar One’s chipotle vodka, made with several kinds of fresh, dried and smoked chilies, is now in stores across the country.
docs.lead_paragraph: Several years ago Lance Winters, the head distiller for Hangar One in California, concocted a limited batch of chipotle vodka by infusing fresh, dried and smoked chilies. The demand outpaced supply. Finally, he has been able to triple the production, and the vodka is now being sold across the country. In addition to japaleños and chipotles (smoked jalapeños), he also uses habaneros for heat, and bell peppers for vegetal richness. The result, 80 proof, has a pale straw color, peppery complexity, haunting smoke and an almost tequilalike greenness to the flavor, making it a spirit to savor on the rocks, to mix in a bloody mary or margarita or to season ceviche.

docs.lead_paragraph: An early-morning fire gutted the historic Élysée Montmartre concert hall in Paris on Tuesday, French officials said. The central stage was untouched, but the second floor partially collapsed, according to news reports. Police said they suspected that the fire was caused by faulty wiring. The hall opened in 1807. Toulouse-Lautrec is reported to have painted several works there, and it is said to have been the birthplace of the cancan. “It is a part of Paris’s identity that has been struck,” said Mayor Bertrand Delanoë, who pledged that it would be rebuilt. No one was hurt in the fire, the authorities said.

docs.lead_paragraph: Maharam Digital Projects — the mural-scaled wallpaper collection from the forward-thinking textile company Maharam — includes work by designers like Marian Bantjes, and artists like James Welling and Marilyn Minter. The fashion icon Paul Smith, who has designed fabrics for Maharam, has also contributed wallpapers. These have tended toward the abstract, but Smith’s latest, Stamp World Map, is a richly detailed collage of letters and stamps from what he calls his “amazing mailbag,” adding that “I love the emphasis and character you can put into handwriting.” People around the world write to Smith, and he answers them all, although he has no idea how to reply to the anonymous American whose fan mail includes actual objects — like a surfboard or a bright pink plastic mannequin — that arrive at Smith’s London studio unboxed and covered with stamps. docs.lead_paragraph: Just a thought on market movements: you often see news stories confidently asserting that factor X was responsible for any given market movement. docs.snippet: Elizabeth Taylor, who died of congestive heart failure today at 79, was the embodiment of modern celebrity glamour.
docs.lead_paragraph: Elizabeth Taylor, who died of congestive heart failure today at 79, was synonymous with jewelry and fragrance. (She famously owned the Cartier and Krupp diamonds, and made a fortune from her various lifestyle perfume concerns.) But Elizabeth Taylor Hilton Wilding Todd Fisher Burton Burton Warner Fortensky was also the embodiment of modern celebrity glamour. Whether being snapped by the ever-present paparazzi or lighting up the screen in her turban-wearing turn as the divinely decadent Sissy Goforth in “Boom!”, she more than looked the part. A lot has been written about the exotic allure she exuded as Cleopatra in 1963, but we have a soft spot for the carnal outfits she wore in her Oscar-winning performance as the call girl Gloria Wandrous in “Butterfield 8,” pictured. What was your favorite Liz Taylor look? Leave your suggestions in the comments below.

headline.main: R.I.P., Elizabeth Taylor (1932-2011)

docs.snippet: Owners in both the N.F.L. and the N.B.A. claim that their businesses are suffering.
docs.lead_paragraph: There’s a pro football team in Washington whose name rhymes — sort of — with “wineskins.” It’s probably best to refer to it this way for now, because the team recently cracked down and made The Washington Post drop the real name from the title of one of its blogs. The rationale seems to be that some other entity, in this case the paper, might be making some unauthorized money by appropriating a brand that belongs to someone else, in this case the team’s owner, Daniel Snyder. No doubt he has the right to do so, but does that mean he’s right to do so? Is it a smart business decision? You’d think that such vigorous policing of a brand’s use in a case like this would threaten to make the brand less appealing to the fans who make that brand valuable in the first place. Apparently not. Snyder has a history of antagonisms — start here, then check out his current lawsuit against The Washington City Paper — and still his is the fourth-most valuable sports team in the world.

headline.main: Owned

docs.abstract: Can the 17-year-old tween idol, beloved by millions as iCarly, turn into a grown-up star without becoming tabloid fodder?
docs.snippet: Can the 17-year-old tween idol, beloved by millions as iCarly, turn into a grown-up star without becoming tabloid fodder?
docs.lead_paragraph: On Veterans Day at Mary Fay Pendleton elementary school on the Camp Pendleton Marine Base, American flags lined the sidewalks. Bunting festooned the windows along with children’s crayoned drawings of tanks, fighter planes and soldiers shooting bullets or throwing grenades. Although the school was closed for the holiday, hundreds of kids and parents had gathered on a playing field to break ground for a new “teaching garden.” The program was sponsored by the American Heart Association and Kelly Meyer, the wife of the Universal Studios president, Ron Meyer. Which explained the improbable presence of Miranda Cosgrove, the 17-year-old star of the hit Nickelodeon show “iCarly.” A photographer stopped her as she walked toward a makeshift stage and asked her to plant a cabbage seedling, but a strand of her long, dark hair fell across her face, ruining his shot. Cosgrove’s smile never dimmed as she scooped up the plant and tried again. This time her hair stayed put. “Perfect,” said the photographer. And it was.

headline.main: The Good Girl, Miranda Cosgrove
headline.print_headline: The Good Girl

docs.abstract: Among the events announced for the Tribeca Film Festival’s Tribeca Talks panel series are discussions with Mr. De Niro and Brian Williams; Alec Baldwin and Doug Liman; and the filmmakers of “A Beautiful Mind.”
docs.snippet: Among the events announced for the Tribeca Film Festival’s Tribeca Talks panel series are discussions with Mr. De Niro and Brian Williams; Alec Baldwin and Doug Liman; and the filmmakers of “A Beautiful Mind.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Jimmy Fallon recently demonstrated that it was possible to extricate a few unscripted words from Robert De Niro, at least within the context of a “Late Night” recreation of the game show “Password.” Next, Mr. Fallon’s NBC colleague Brian Williams will attempt to coax further spontaneous utterances out of Mr. De Niro, the soft-spoken screen actor and co-founder of the Tribeca Film Festival, at a one-on-one discussion that will be held as part of the festival’s Tribeca Talks panel series, its organizers said on Wednesday. In addition to Mr. Williams’s interview of Mr. De Niro, which will take place on April 23 at the Borough of Manhattan Community College, other announced events include a conversation between Doug Liman, the “Bourne Identity” director, and Alec Baldwin, the “30 Rock” star; a discussion between the director Martin Scorsese and the Malian filmmaker Souleymane Cissé; and a 10th-anniversary screening of “A Beautiful Mind” that will be followed by a conversation with that film’s director, Ron Howard, producer Brian Grazer, and the screenwriter, Akiva Goldsman. The film’s math consultant, Dave Bayer, Sylvia Nasar, the author of the book “A Beautiful Mind,” and Brian Greene, the theoretical physicist and mathematician will also participate. The Tribeca Film Festival runs from April 20 to May 1, and more information about its screenings and events can be found at tribecafilm.com.

headline.main: Robert De Niro to Get a Good Talking-To at Tribeca Festival

docs.abstract: A.P.C.’s latest edition of quilts  are at once graphically modern and sentimentally nostalgic.
docs.snippet: A.P.C.’s latest edition of quilts  are at once graphically modern and sentimentally nostalgic.
docs.lead_paragraph: A.P.C. does not, as far as we know, stand for A Prairie (Home) Companion, but the 25-year-old brand’s latest edition of quilts has us wondering. The seven styles — made from 50 collections’ worth of unused tweed, wool, corduroy and printed cotton scrap fabric — are at once graphically modern and sentimentally nostalgic. “My mother made me a log cabin quilt from leftover fabric that we were given while I was working at Kenzo,” says the A.P.C. founder Jean Touitou. “So, the idea came quite naturally.” And while quilts are very of the moment — think Rodarte’s prairie-inspired collection for fall 2011 — according to Touitou, these are pieces that are designed to last. “What’s important is passing on culture, it’s like blues or cooking,” he says. “Perhaps it will fix some memories for people. Or simply they’ll have a hell of a graceful piece of popular art where they live.”

headline.main: A Prairie Home Companion | A.P.C. Quilts

docs.lead_paragraph: When I do TV pundit shows, I am usually placed on the right facing the host so when I turn to speak with my more liberal partner, I end up exposing my right cheek to the camera. I never really thought about the significance of this. But in the journal Laterality: Assymetries of the Body, Brain & Cognition, Annukka Lindell and Nicola Savill point out that the face expresses emotion asymmetrically. The left cheek is more emotionally expressive whereas the right cheek is more passive.

headline.main: Turning the Other Cheek. It Works.

docs.abstract: The pianist Maurizio Pollini has canceled a United States recital tour because of illness, Carnegie Hall said in a statement on  Wednesday.
docs.snippet: The pianist Maurizio Pollini has canceled a United States recital tour because of illness, Carnegie Hall said in a statement on  Wednesday.
docs.lead_paragraph: The pianist Maurizio Pollini has canceled a United States recital tour because of illness, Carnegie Hall said in a statement on Wednesday. Mr. Pollini was to have played at Carnegie on Sunday and on April 4. The pianist Jeremy Denk will perform in his place on Sunday; a substitute has yet to be named for the April 4 concert. Mr. Pollini also had stops in Princeton, N.J., and Chicago. He previously canceled appearances this month with the Boston Symphony Orchestra in Boston and at Carnegie. A hall spokesman said he did not know the nature of Mr. Pollini’s illness, and the pianist’s New York-based manager did not immediately return a phone call. Mr. Denk will play Charles Ives’s Piano Sonata No. 2 ( “Concord”) and Bach’s “Goldberg” Variations, which he performed just last month at Carnegie’s smaller Zankel Hall.

headline.main: Maurizio Pollini Cancels United States Recital Tour

docs.lead_paragraph: In the age of YouTube, Pandora and Spotify, fans can watch millions of videos or listen to endless hours of music for free. But do those services make significant money for artists and record companies? Those questions became all the more interesting last week with “Friday,” a song by Rebecca Black, a 13-year-old amateur from California whose YouTube video became a viral sensation. With heavily Auto-Tuned vocals and lines like “Tomorrow is Saturday/And Sunday comes afterwards,” critics abhorred it. Yet it had racked up more than 38.5 million views by Wednesday afternoon, and the single was slowly climbing iTunes’s posted popularity charts.

docs.snippet: Our strategic incoherence and its consequences.
docs.lead_paragraph: This administration’s Libya policy has grown steadily more baffling with every day that we’ve spent at war. On the one hand, it’s clear that the Obama White House desires nothing more than to hand responsibility for this military operation over to France and Britain posthaste, and that the president has absolutely no intention of committing American ground forces to the shores of Tripoli. On the other hand, it’s also clear that it may well take more than an air bombardment to remove Qaddafi’s regime from power, which is the outcome that France is more or less explicitly pursuing, and that Britain and the United States are informally committed to as well. So where does this leave us? Adam Garfinkle minces no words:

docs.abstract: Elizabeth Taylor was a survivor, and it was that survival that helped separate her from many other old Hollywood stars.
docs.snippet: Elizabeth Taylor was a survivor, and it was that survival that helped separate her from many other old Hollywood stars.
docs.lead_paragraph: The last movie star died Wednesday. By the time Elizabeth Taylor left this mortal coil at 79, she had cheated death with a long line of infirmities that had repeatedly put her in the hospital — and on front pages across the world — and in 1961 left her with a tracheotomy scar on a neck more accustomed to diamonds. The tracheotomy was the result of a bout with pneumonia that left her gasping for air and it returned her to the big, bountiful, hungry life that was one of her greatest roles. It was a minor incision (later, she had surgery to remove the scar), but it’s easy to think of it as some kind of war wound for a life lived so magnificently.

headline.main: Lust for Life: Movies, Men, Melodramas

docs.lead_paragraph: The country’s highest court has upheld the death sentences of seven people in the far western region of Xinjiang who were convicted of murders and robberies aimed at raising money for a terrorist plot, state media reported Wednesday. Three others who had been sentenced to death were given a two-year reprieve, which often leads to life in prison. The attacks in Kashgar left nine people dead, the newspaper The Xinjiang Daily said. It did not cite the ethnicity of the defendants, but the names suggested that they were Uighurs, who make up a majority of Kashgar’s population. Calls to the People’s Intermediate Court in Kashgar rang unanswered Wednesday; the Supreme People’s Court typically does not release details of its rulings.

docs.abstract: Mr. Harris, an Academy Award nominee for “Apollo 13″ and “Pollock,” will play Mr. McCain in a television movie about the 2008 presidential campaign.
docs.snippet: Mr. Harris, an Academy Award nominee for “Apollo 13″ and “Pollock,” will play Mr. McCain in a television movie about the 2008 presidential campaign.
docs.lead_paragraph: Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona, made a pretty convincing Senator John McCain when he appeared as himself in “Wedding Crashers” and on “Saturday Night Live,” but HBO Films has decided to go a different route in casting for its coming television-movie “Game Change.” On Wednesday evening HBO said that it had chosen Ed Harris, the Academy Award-nominated star of “Apollo 13,” “Pollock,” “The Truman Show” and “The Hours,” to play Mr. McCain in the film, which is adapted from the book of the same title by John Heilemann and Mark Halperin. The film will chronicle Mr. McCain’s 2008 presidential campaign starting with his selection of Sarah Palin as his running mate. HBO previously announced that Julianne Moore (of “The Kids Are All Right”) would play Ms. Palin in the film, which will be directed by Jay Roach (“Dinner for Schmucks”) and written by Danny Strong. Mr. Roach and Mr. Strong previously collaborated on the HBO movie “Recount,” about the backroom battles that followed the 2000 presidential election. A broadcast date for “Game Change” has not yet been announced.

headline.main: HBO Votes for Ed Harris to Play John McCain

docs.lead_paragraph: Wednesday night’s shindig (nice word … mmm …) for Vanessa Traina and her Maje collaboration was relaxed and fun. I didn’t need to go to the hairdresser, after all. It started on the seventh floor of Barneys, with a D.J., and the arrivals of Ashley and Mary-Kate Olsen, in a great-looking fur jacket, though I liked the look of Ashley’s broad-shoulder beige coat over a long black Row dress; then the designers Alexander Wang, Joseph Altuzarra and Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez of Proenza Schouler. People were talking about Elizabeth Taylor, Carine Roitfeld’s appointment as a guest editor/stylist for Barneys and places they had recently been (other than fashion shows), and eyeing a Maje blazer with satin lapels, as if to say, “Should I or shouldn’t I?” Ms. Traina, whose sisters Victoria and Samantha also attended, had on a blazer and skinny pants, with a cutaway Balenciaga top that draped in the front. Dinner was down the slushy street, at Caprice.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Color Me Obsessed” is just about the perfect title for a new documentary about the Replacements. The movie’s tag line is also promising: “The potentially true story of the last best band.” And yet I was a little surprised to learn that the Replacements themselves are not really in the film. Instead, the movie is a parade of 40-something (and older) ex-rockers and critics reminiscing ecstatically about the glory days. (Those would be the years 1981 to 1987.) A colleague (and huge ’Mats fan) objected, “If I want to hear a bunch of guys talk about how great the Replacements were, I’ll go hang out in a record store!” He paused as the realization sunk in: there are no more record stores. “Color Me Obsessed” will have to do.

headline.main: The Replacements Approach to the Replacements

docs.abstract: Seemingly overnight, whole swaths of downtown and nearby neighborhoods — notably South Lake Union and the Pike-Pine Corridor — have transformed themselves into enclaves of restaurants, bars and galleries.
docs.snippet: Seemingly overnight, whole swaths of downtown and nearby neighborhoods — notably South Lake Union and the Pike-Pine Corridor — have transformed themselves into enclaves of restaurants, bars and galleries.
docs.lead_paragraph: SPRING comes early to Seattle and lasts long. By the end of February, the rains relent and pastel shades of plum and narcissus initiate a progression of color and scent that lasts months. But new flora is not the only thing popping out of the ground in Seattle these days. Seemingly overnight, whole swatches of downtown and close-in neighborhoods — notably South Lake Union and the Pike-Pine Corridor — have transformed themselves into vibrant enclaves of restaurants, bars and galleries. With so many converted and repurposed buildings, Seattle’s cityscape is starting to look as layered as the wardrobes of its inhabitants. The tarry pitch of the timber port never disappeared; it just got plastered over with grunge flannel, tech money, yuppie coffee, Pacific Rim flavors, and more recently the backyard chickens and chard of urban pioneers. Don’t let a passing shower keep you from entering the mix. This is one of the rare American cities where you can be outdoors year-round without either shivering or sweating.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Seattle

ABC and its comedy line-up finished in third place over all, benefiting largely from solid ratings for “Modern Family” at 9 (10.8 million). docs.abstract: “Illegal,” by Olivier Masset-Depasse, follows the desperate struggles of an immigrant trying to stay in her adopted land.
docs.snippet: “Illegal,” by Olivier Masset-Depasse, follows the desperate struggles of an immigrant trying to stay in her adopted land.
docs.lead_paragraph: Ripped from the headlines or a pool of similarly themed movies, the fiction film “Illegal” traces the ups and increasing downs of an immigrant’s struggles to stay in her adopted land. At once high-minded, sincere and frustrating, it opens with its central character, a Russian immigrant, Tania (Anne Coesens), reading a letter denying her residency in Belgium. Facing immediate deportation with her young son, Ivan (Alexandre Gontcharov), Tania reacts with the rash desperation that characterizes many of her subsequent actions: she takes an iron and begins burning her fingertips, obliterating one proof of her identity.

docs.lead_paragraph: Every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way, according to Tolstoy, except in mainstream movie comedies where many unhappy families are exactly alike. The latest proof is “Peep World,” a family circus of dysfunction that’s so familiar you may feel tempted to place bets on how everything will shake out, and painless enough that you might not resent doing so. That’s particularly the case whenever Michael C. Hall and Judy Greer, as a troubled married couple, show up and, by virtue of their professionalism, help to distract you from the flat jokes, ethnic clichés and formulaic relationships noisily vying for your attention.

docs.abstract: Catherine Deneuve and Gérard Depardieu join forces in the 1970s-era comedy “Potiche,” about a trophy wife who must run the family business.
docs.snippet: Catherine Deneuve and Gérard Depardieu join forces in the 1970s-era comedy “Potiche,” about a trophy wife who must run the family business.
docs.lead_paragraph: The experience of watching François Ozon’s “Potiche (Trophy Wife)” is, in many ways, more like attending a theatrical matinee than like going out for a night at the movies. This is not only because Mr. Ozon’s source is a once popular, slightly musty play from the 1970s (by the writing team of Pierre Barillet and Jean-Pierre Grédy), which he has lovingly refurbished with impeccable attention to period décor and present-day sensitivities. Mr. Ozon, a prolific filmmaker, has also, perhaps intentionally, approximated the stodgy good cheer that often distinguishes lavish, star-studded stage revivals of beloved old chestnuts. You suspect, before long, that there is no strong reason for this production to exist, but it is reasonably good fun all the same.

docs.lead_paragraph: If you sometimes feel that Germany has contributed more than its share of provocative, irreverent artists to 20th- and 21st-century art, you may be right. During the postwar era, at least, we might credit an art-academy system that encourages independence, or maybe a society that remains somewhat more rigid than many of its Western counterparts.

docs.abstract: What the world’s ‘most famous newspaper correspondent’ saw, and reported, while covering the Civil War.
docs.snippet: What the world’s ‘most famous newspaper correspondent’ saw, and reported, while covering the Civil War.
docs.lead_paragraph: On the night before William Howard Russell left London for New York, he dined at the Garrick Club with William Makepeace Thackeray. Charles Dickens, Anthony Trollope and many other leading lights of English culture and society also belonged to the private establishment. Although admitted to the Bar, it was as a correspondent for The Times of London that Russell established his reputation. His fame came from his dogged coverage of the Crimean War and, at its conclusion in 1856, he returned a hero. His dispatches brought the war home to readers. He wrote with clarity and vitality about the grandeur and the horror of battle. He followed that with an equally vivid account of the Sepoy Rebellion in India. People called him a “war correspondent,” perhaps the first, but he rejected the label and departed on March 3 for the brewing conflict in America as “special correspondent” for The Times.

headline.main: The Special Correspondent

docs.abstract: Lanford Wilson reflected the disenchantment that came to pervade the United States in the 1960s and 1970s, but his work exuded a sentimentality that seemed to come from an earlier time.
docs.snippet: Lanford Wilson reflected the disenchantment that came to pervade the United States in the 1960s and 1970s, but his work exuded a sentimentality that seemed to come from an earlier time.
docs.lead_paragraph: Lanford Wilson liked losers. This is not to say that he gloried, masochistically, in defeat. But as a playwright, he knew that the most poignant drama often radiates from people’s failure to connect with one another, with their aspirations and with their own feelings. In this sense, you could say he was an heir to Tennessee Williams, another dramatist who saw the poetry in withered hopes and ideals tenuously sustained against a world of denial. If his characters lacked the complexity of Williams’s greatest creations, they possessed some of the same vital glow, that of a self-consuming bonfire in a chilly twilight.

headline.main: Playwright Infusing His Losers With Love

docs.lead_paragraph: The battle over a state law curbing the union rights of public workers is headed for the State Supreme Court after a lower court declined to weigh in on the issue. The lower court, the Wisconsin Court of Appeals, said the issues involved were so fundamental — involving a clash between the state’s open meetings law and the separation of legislative and judicial powers — that it made sense to send the case straight to state’s highest court. Last Friday, a judge in Dane County blocked the law while she considered a lawsuit that accuses Republican lawmakers of violating open meetings laws by failing to give adequate notice of the vote on the union law. The state had asked the appeals court to throw out that order. Also Thursday, an Indiana prosecutor said one of his deputies had resigned after admitting that he sent an e-mail to Gov. Scott Walker of Wisconsin suggesting that Mr. Walker fake an attack on himself to discredit the unions. The prosecutor, Brad Cooper of Johnson County, said the deputy, Carlos Lam, acknowledged that he sent an e-mail, which was obtained by The Associated Press. It said: “If you could employ an associate who pretends to be sympathetic to the unions’ cause to physically attack you (or even use a firearm against you), you could discredit the public unions.”

headline.main: Wisconsin: No Ruling on Union Law

docs.lead_paragraph: The United Nations human rights body voted Thursday for the appointment of an investigator to monitor and report on Iran in response to its crackdown on political dissent. The Human Rights Council in Geneva voted 20 to 7, with 11 abstentions, in favor of the resolution co-sponsored by the United States and Sweden to appoint the investigator. Earlier, the council heard a report by the United Nations secretary general, Ban Ki-moon, in which he said Iran’s leaders had intensified their crackdown on political opponents, activists and journalists and noted a “dramatic surge” in the number of executions since the start of 2011. The United States ambassador, Eileen Donahoe, hailed the vote as a “seminal moment” for the council. Iran condemned the resolution as an abuse of the council.

docs.abstract: Shouldn’t we have much more advanced nuclear “machines”?
docs.snippet: Shouldn’t we have much more advanced nuclear “machines”?
docs.lead_paragraph: The imperiled Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant in Japan dates from the 1960s. Forty-plus years may not be a long time when it comes to radioactive decay — 300 years to go for the Switzerland-size contaminated area around Chernobyl — but it can feel like close to forever when you think about the engineering and technological advances since the pre-moon-landing days. Steven Chu, the secretary of energy, says that the 23 American reactors (more than 20 percent of our reactor fleet, by the way) built according to the same design as the Fukushima Daiichi station are continually “upgraded” to ensure their safety. But still. As one of our contributing writers, Jon Gertner, put it a few years ago, “Nuclear power plants are arguably the most complicated machines in the history of civilization.” Even as that partly hints at why their failures can be so catastrophic, it also prompts the question: Shouldn’t we have more than upgrades by now? Shouldn’t we have much more advanced nuclear “machines” already?

headline.main: Atomic Ages

docs.lead_paragraph: Reunited and it feels so good: four members of the vintage-1990s rock band Hole, which never got along as smoothly as any  Peaches & Herb song, are planning to reconvene on Monday at the New Directors/New Films series to see a documentary about the former Hole drummer Patty Schemel, the Museum of Modern Art and the Film Society of Lincoln Center said. A screening at MoMA of “Hit So Hard,” directed by P. David Ebersole, is set to be visited by its subject, Ms. Schemel, as well as the guitarist Eric Erlandson and the bassist Melissa Auf der Maur, not to mention a certain idiosyncratic front woman and fashion plate named Courtney Love. If we sound a little surprised by the gathering (which the film series organizers say is the first time these four musicians have been together at a public event in 13 years), consider such past events in the history of Hole as: Ms. Schemel’s departure from the group in 1998 and the band’s dissolution in 2002; Ms. Love’s announcement of a Hole reunion in 2009 that seemed to surprise Ms. Auf der Mar; Mr. Erlandson’s remarks that “there is no Hole without me” and Ms. Love’s online reply that Hole is “MY Band” and “MY name.” A Q. and A. with Mr. Ebersole and the band members is set to follow the screening; there was no mention of whether it would be conducted from within a steel cage.

docs.snippet: How the scientific attempt to describe the underlying order of the cosmos played out in the life of Isaac Newton.
docs.lead_paragraph: London before the mid-1600s was a general calamity. The streets were full of thieves, murderers and human waste. Death was everywhere: doctors were hapless, adults lived to about age 30, children died like flies. In 1665, plague moved into the city, killing sometimes 6,000 people a week. In 1666, an unstoppable fire burned the city to the ground; the bells of St. Paul’s melted. Londoners thought that the terrible voice of God was “roaring in the City,” one witness wrote, and they would do best to accept the horror, calculate their sins, pray for guidance and await retribution.

headline.main: What Newton Gave Us

docs.abstract: The journalist Peter Godwin’s latest chronicle of the horrors of Zimbabwe under Mugabe.
docs.snippet: The journalist Peter Godwin’s latest chronicle of the horrors of Zimbabwe under Mugabe.
docs.lead_paragraph: Peter Godwin has carved out a niche as a skillful chronicler of politics and war in his native Zimbabwe. His 1996 memoir, “Mukiwa: A White Boy in Africa,” was an affecting account of his coming-of-age in white-minority-ruled Rhodesia, where his father managed a factory and his mother, a physician, operated a rural health clinic. The story climaxed with the outbreak of the civil war that would bring the guerrilla leader Robert Mugabe to power — and with the accidental killing of Godwin’s elder sister by Rhodesian troops at a roadblock. “When a Crocodile Eats the Sun: A Memoir of Africa,” published in 2007, picked up the narrative with Mugabe’s evolution into a brutal dictator who stomped on the opposition, evicted thousands of white farmers in a violent land reform program and plunged his country into ruin. Now Godwin has written the third installment of what might be called his Zimbabwe trilogy. In “The Fear: Robert Mugabe and the Martyrdom of Zimbabwe,” he documents the 2008 presidential election and its aftermath, when Mugabe unleashed ruling-party militias in a savage campaign to keep his hold on power.

headline.main: African Tyrant

docs.lead_paragraph: In the summer of 1937, with the Dodgers holding down their familiar spot near the bottom of the National League, the cartoonist Willard Mullin drew the unforgettable image of the “Brooklyn Bum” — a potbellied, cigar-chomping hobo who combined the cheerful ineptitude of the players and the goofy optimism of their fans. Named for the singular “dodging” skills of pedestrians in a borough crammed with trolley lines, the Dodgers hadn’t captured a pennant since 1920, and had never won a World Series. “Brooklyn?” roared Bill Terry, manager of the hated New York Giants. “Is Brooklyn still in the league?” Dodger fans were largely immune to this abuse. Their addiction had taught them patience and humility — like belonging to a religion whose one flaw was an unreachable promised land. From Bay Ridge to Brownsville, from Flatbush to Coney Island, it was always “Wait till next year.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Throughout Alan Heathcock’s impressive first story collection, “Volt,” trouble appears in biblical proportions in the imaginary rural town of Krafton: floods, homicides, fires and fratricides are among the catastrophes to confront the blue-collar citizenry. For Heathcock, suffering is everyone’s fate, a point he drives home repeatedly. When a teenager in one story helps burn the body of a man his father has killed in a senseless fight, he thinks of “all the fires the world has ever seen, fires from wars, fires from bombs,” and concludes that the lingering remains of all that smoke is “now just the air we breathe.” In other words, sorrow and strife are permanent parts of the human condition.

docs.lead_paragraph: Popular song gained an indelible image in 1935, when Édith Piaf, France’s fabled “Little Sparrow,” first stood onstage in a plain black dress, a rat’s nest of dark hair topping her weary eyes. Singing in a piquant tone with a thick vibrato, she poured out tales of working-class lives and endurance pushed to the brink, usually by love. Face, hands and voice were all she needed to bring her playlets to life. One of her trademarks, “L’Accordéoniste,” was written for her in 1940. As she sang of a prostitute whose musician lover went off to war and never returned, Piaf rocked her arms through the air manically to the rhythm of his playing; she caressed her stomach as though remembering how he felt against her.

docs.snippet: Alex von Tunzelmann reconstructs an era when Cuba, Haiti and the Dominican Republic were cold war battlegrounds.
docs.lead_paragraph: For a historian wishing to chronicle American foreign policy foolishness, there is no more promising territory than the Western Hemisphere. One could begin with the 1823 Monroe Doctrine, by which the United States reserved the right to intervene militarily in the region, and then look just about anywhere down through the years for examples of shameful behavior. In “Red Heat,” Alex von Tunzelmann concentrates on just one area, the Caribbean, and mainly on one decade, the 1960s. In those years, the United States promoted political assassinations, turned a blind eye to horrific brutality and repression by local tyrants, sponsored an invasion of Cuba and dispatched 23,000 soldiers and Marines to the Dominican Republic in order to prevent the establishment of a government there it feared would be unfriendly.

docs.lead_paragraph: Henning Mankell has spoken: Detective Chief Inspector Kurt Wallander has solved his last case. Making this news more bitter, the alcoholic, diabetic, antisocial and perpetually dour Swedish detective is at his gloomy best in THE TROUBLED MAN (Knopf, $26.95). After his colleagues on the Ystad police force gave him a 50th-birthday party, Wallander started keeping a record of all the people he knew of who were now dead, a morbid task that he abandoned after the 10th suicide. Five years later, he bought a house near the sea and acquired a dog, indicating some improvement in his mental health. But having reached the age of 60, Wallander has become lonely and despondent. “His life was now centered increasingly on recalling things from the past that he now realized he missed,” Mankell observes, in the melancholy words of Laurie Thompson’s translation.

docs.abstract: Six letters by Frédéric Chopin went on display this week at the Chopin museum in Warsaw after having been lost from view since the early  years of World War II.
docs.snippet: Six letters by Frédéric Chopin went on display this week at the Chopin museum in Warsaw after having been lost from view since the early  years of World War II.
docs.lead_paragraph: They speak of his friends, the troubled composition of his Cello Sonata, his favorite hot chocolate. Six letters by Frédéric Chopin went on display this week at the Chopin museum in Warsaw after having been lost from view since the early years of World War II. The missives date from 1845 to 1848, a year before Chopin’s death, and were written from Paris and Nohant in central France — the childhood home of George Sand, Chopin’s lover — to the composer’s family in Warsaw. It was a time of considerable turmoil in the Chopin-Sand domestic arrangement. The letters were in the hands of Laura Ciechomska, a grandniece of Chopin, until at least 1939, a museum curator, Alicja Knast, said, according to The Associated Press. They resurfaced in 2003, and the museum later acquired them, The Associated Press said.

headline.main: Frédéric Chopin Letters Go On Display in Warsaw

docs.abstract: Scribner has acquired the rights to publish “The _____ Epic Twitter Quest of @MayorEmanuel,” a book based on the profanity-laced Twitter feed.
docs.snippet: Scribner has acquired the rights to publish “The _____ Epic Twitter Quest of @MayorEmanuel,” a book based on the profanity-laced Twitter feed.
docs.lead_paragraph: Add another entry to the growing publishing genre of Twitter lit. Scribner has acquired the rights to publish a book based on the profanity-laced Twitter feed written by a fake Rahm Emanuel, later revealed to be Dan Sinker. Mr. Sinker, the founding editor of the culture magazine “Punk Planet” and an assistant professor at Columbia College in Chicago, was anonymously behind the much-followed Twitter feed until he revealed his identity in The Atlantic last month. The book will “compile the tweets, annotate them and include Sinker’s first-person account of the phenomenon that has attracted legions of followers and media attention,” his publisher said in a statement on Friday. Scribner, an imprint of Simon & Schuster, plans to release the book — with a foreword by Biz Stone, a founder of Twitter — later this year.

headline.main: A Book for @MayorEmanuel

docs.abstract: That which doesn’t kill us can make us stronger. Head injuries a case in point.
docs.snippet: That which doesn’t kill us can make us stronger. Head injuries a case in point.
docs.lead_paragraph: None of us is looking to sustain a serious head injury, but Janelle Jones and some colleagues conducted a survey of 630 people who had sustained serious injuries with the help of Headway UK. She found that survivors of serious head injuries are much more satisfied with their lives than others. They seem to regard themselves as survivors. They tell stories about their lives that emphasize resilience and bouncing back. What’s more, they relied on strong social support networks to get through their injuries. The write up of the study in Psychology and Health carries the apt title: “That Which Doesn’t Kill Us Can Make Us Stronger.”

headline.main: Resilience

docs.abstract: In our latest Spring Travel issue of T Magazine: how to explore the world with efficiency and grace.
docs.snippet: In our latest Spring Travel issue of T Magazine: how to explore the world with efficiency and grace.
docs.lead_paragraph: The latest Spring Travel issue of T magazine heads to Haiti with the actor Sean Penn, who spent most of the last year in the country coordinating a remarkably effective relief effort. Zoë Heller’s profile helps us see the beauty beneath the devastation and the generosity behind the usually guarded star. The writer Wells Tower also takes a timely journey, this one through Humboldt County, the cannabis-growing hub of California (much in the news recently) with a lovably cantankerous local culture and an impossibly gorgeous landscape. Nature is also the lure in Newfoundland, Canada, which, as Mark Schatzker learns, is perhaps the best place to catch and eat a wild Atlantic salmon, a fish most of us have only eaten farmed. Elsewhere in the issue are more cerebral pleasures, as in Trieste, a legendary Italian redoubt for thinkers and flâneurs, and Beirut, Lebanon, where Joumana Haddad is creating a stir with her erotic writing — as well as plenty of sybaritic pursuits: a luxurious new boot-camp spa in Laguna, Calif.; a revived, post-recession London filled with new restaurants, shops and bars; and a lively music scene revolves around the beer halls and nightclubs of Hamburg, Germany, a playground forever enshrined by the Beatles. See all stories from the issue >>

headline.main: T’s Spring Travel Issue

docs.lead_paragraph: “Histoire du Soldat” should be “read, played and danced,” wrote its composer, Stravinsky, and its author, Charles-Ferdinand Ramuz, when the work was first performed in Lausanne, Switzerland, in 1918. And although the piece is often presented as a musical suite, those instructions have frequently been taken to heart. With its crisp narrative — a soldier sells his violin (and thus his soul) to the Devil, fights to win it back, but ultimately loses it again — its dance-rich, jazz-influenced melodies; and its dramatic text, “Soldat” (“The Soldier’s Tale”) offers abundant collaborative possibilities.

docs.abstract: The Broadway musical’s new script jettisons the director Julie Taymor’s Geek Chorus of narrators and reduces her villainess Arachne to a supporting character.
docs.snippet: The Broadway musical’s new script jettisons the director Julie Taymor’s Geek Chorus of narrators and reduces her villainess Arachne to a supporting character.
docs.lead_paragraph: Cast members of “Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark” held their first organized reading on Friday of the Broadway musical’s new script, which jettisons the director Julie Taymor’s Geek Chorus of narrators and reduces her villainess Arachne to a supporting character, according to two members of the production who attended the reading. The new script beefs up the role of another villain, the Green Goblin (right, played by Patrick Page, battling Reeve Carney as Peter Parker/Spider-Man), who proved popular with focus groups that the producers convened after the onslaught of negative reviews by theater critics. Most of the changes will be implemented during the show’s hiatus, which starts April 19, according to the two production members, who would only speak anonymously because the producers do not want the changes discussed publicly. On Thursday, the producers said that the choreographer Chase Brock would stage new musical numbers. Mr. Brock, 27, is best known for his choreography on a popular video game, the Broadway Experience. He takes over from Daniel Ezralow. The producers ousted Ms. Taymor this month; Mr. Ezralow said at the time that he was directly assured that he would continue with the show. Ben Brantley, the chief theater critic of The New York Times, wrote in February that the musical may “rank among the worst” in Broadway history and that Mr. Ezralow’s choreography was “pure vintage MTV.”

headline.main: A New Script for ‘Spider-Man’: Goodbye Geeks

docs.snippet: A Manhattan drug store with a beer counter opens while a video rental store in Brooklyn closes up.
docs.lead_paragraph: DUANE READE ranks pretty high on the list of character-killing (if useful) additions to a neighborhood. But the Duane Reade that opened this month on Broadway at 72nd Street has an unusual distinction: It is the second in the city with a beer counter, called Brew York City. It’s not quite a bar, because the not-quite-a-bartender who stands behind it can’t pour glasses of beer for customers to sip while filling prescriptions or perusing the shampoo selection. Instead, he sells growlers, refillable glass bottles, for $3.99. And for $7.99, he fills them with one of nine varieties of beer on tap, like Sixpoint Sweet Action or Ithaca Apricot Wheat. Last year, a Duane Reade in Williamsburg, Brooklyn, became the city’s first with a beer counter. It was such a hit, said Richard Ruiz, the Broadway store’s manager, that it is being repeated. “Everyone slows down when they pass this section,” said Julio Vega, who was manning the counter one recent afternoon. Across the aisle: bags full of potato chips and pretzels.

docs.snippet: The central government in Beijing is tightening budgets for “overseas junkets, receptions and cars to fight against extravagance in 2011,” according to the state news agency.
docs.lead_paragraph: The central government in Beijing is tightening budgets for “overseas junkets, receptions and cars to fight against extravagance in 2011,” according to a report by Xinhua, the state news agency. The report indicated that government corruption continued to be a major concern among Chinese, and that some in the central government realize the ubiquitous image of corrupt officialdom is eroding the confidence of Chinese people. Xinhua, citing a meeting on Wednesday of the State Council, the Chinese cabinet, said that the central government would report the final budget for those expenses to the National People’s Congress, a rubber-stamp legislature, and make the accounting available for public scrutiny. Xinhua cited one official saying a crackdown on extravagant spending had saved the nation nearly $900 million last year. It is unclear whether such crackdowns have really had any significant impact on corruption and waste.

headline.main: China: Cutting Frills From Junkets

docs.lead_paragraph: THE difference was apparent from the moment the bread basket arrived. During an enjoyable lunch at Tappo, an Italian restaurant in downtown Stamford that opened last October, the fresh Tuscan bread had been crusty, with a light, textured interior; at a weeknight dinner it tasted store-bought. Given that the unfiltered extra-virgin olive oil accompanying the bread — made with Coratina olives, our waiter said — was excellent both times of day, I would have considered the bread an exception, a slow-night slip-up. But then came the fried baby artichokes. Stippled with fresh parsley and sheer shavings of Grana Padano, they had been crisp and full of flavor at lunch; at dinner the dish was listless.

docs.lead_paragraph: Gaston Caperton, who as president of the College Board is the ultimate proctor of the SAT and Advanced Placement exams, announced Friday that he would step down in June 2012. Mr. Caperton, 71, a former Democratic governor of West Virginia, has led the College Board since 1999. A search for his successor is expected to begin soon, the board said. Mr. Caperton has presided over a period of enormous growth at the College Board, as the number of students who took one of its exams or its courses grew to over 7 million last year, compared with 3 million in 1999, the organization said. Among his accomplishments, the board said, was tripling the number of low-income students who took at least one Advanced Placement course. In that time, though, the SAT has lost ground to its chief rival, the ACT, a college entrance exam that tends to measure more of what students learn in the classroom than the SAT, which can be more of a yardstick of analytical skills.

docs.lead_paragraph: In an embarrassment for Warner Brothers, which spent over $100 million to make and market the fantasy thriller “Sucker Punch,” an inexpensive children’s movie from 20th Century Fox — “Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Rodrick Rules” — was No. 1 at the weekend box office. “Rodrick,” with Zachary Gordon and Laine MacNeil, above, is the second in the “Wimpy Kid” series. It was produced for about $21 million and sold an estimated $24.4 million in tickets at North American theaters over the weekend, according to Hollywood.com, which compiles box office statistics. “Sucker Punch,” directed by Zack Snyder and partly financed by Legendary Pictures, was second with about $19 million. A forceful marketing campaign could not overcome abysmal reviews and a lack of interest (aside from young men) for the story line, in which a group of scantily clad, gun-toting women try to escape from an insane asylum. “Limitless” (Relativity Media) was third in its second week with about $15.2 million for a new total of $41.3 million. “The Lincoln Lawyer” (Lionsgate) was fourth, selling $11 million for a two-week total of about $30 million. “Rango” (Paramount Pictures) was fifth, with $9.8 million to lift its four-week total to about $106.4 million.

docs.lead_paragraph: Many indigenous dance forms are reflections of the same human impulses: to tell stories, to explain human history, to express relationships to the natural world and to honor ancestors and the gods. docs.lead_paragraph: Bret Michaels, the lead singer of the band Poison, filed a lawsuit against Tony Award Productions, CBS and others, claiming that they were responsible for the accident that lead to his near-fatal brain hemorrhage last year, according to The Hollywood Reporter. Mr. Michaels was treated for a broken nose and received stitches for a split lip after he was struck by a descending backdrop while exiting the stage after a performance at the 2009 Tony Awards. In the suit, filed on Friday in Los Angeles County Superior Court, Mr. Michaels alleged that he was not properly informed of how to leave the stage safely, which led to his injury and eventually to his brain hemorrhage last April. Representatives from Tony Award Productions and CBS have not responded.
